Use this when a small number of accounts are worth a coordinated effort. ABM works when sales and marketing run one plan per account (or cluster) with the same message, not when marketing runs ads at a list.

## Inputs

- Target accounts and why each matters.
- Research per account (or run an account research brief).
- Budget, team and timeline.

## The play

### 1. Tier the program
| Tier | Accounts | Effort |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1:1 | 5-15 | Custom insight, content and plays per account |
| 1:few | 20-100 in clusters of 5-15 | Content per industry or shared problem |
| 1:many | 100-1,000 | Segment-level messaging, targeted ads and outbound |

### 2. Map the buying group
Per account: economic buyer, champion candidates, evaluators, users, blockers. Five to ten names for 1:1 accounts.

### 3. Write the account insight
What is happening at the account that makes your value urgent: strategy, triggers, pains, initiatives. Then the value hypothesis: "Because <insight>, <account> could <outcome> by <how>, worth about <impact>." Read [references/abm-plan-template.md](references/abm-plan-template.md) for the full one-page plan.

### 4. Plan plays by stage
| Stage | Goal | Plays |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unaware | Get known by the buying group | Targeted ads to the group, executive content, events, insight-led outreach |
| Engaged | Start conversations | Personalised outreach to 3+ people, custom insight piece, invite to a roundtable |
| Opportunity | Win the evaluation | Business case built with the champion, executive sponsor, peer references |
| Customer | Expand | Value review, new-team plays |

Sales and marketing actions for each stage share one calendar.

### 5. Measure what matters
Engaged contacts per account, meetings with the buying group, opportunities created, pipeline and win rate versus non-ABM accounts. Impressions and clicks are inputs, not results.

## What good looks like

- Each Tier 1 account has a specific insight a rep could open a conversation with.
- Three or more people per account engaged before an opportunity is opened.
- Sales and marketing review accounts together every two weeks.
- The common mistake is "ABM" that is just ads to a target list, with no account insight and no sales follow-through.

## Rules

- MUST write an account-specific insight for every 1:1 account.
- MUST coordinate sales and marketing touches on one calendar.
- NEVER use personal data about individuals beyond their professional role and public work.

## Example prompts

- "Build a 1:1 ABM plan for our 10 enterprise targets in logistics."
- "Cluster these 60 accounts for a 1:few program and write the message per cluster."
- "How do we measure whether our ABM program is working?"

INSIGHT
What's happening: <strategy, triggers, initiatives, with sources>
Value hypothesis: Because <insight>, <account> could <outcome> by <how>, worth ~<impact>.

BUYING GROUP
Name | Title | Role (EB/champion/evaluator/user/blocker) | Status | Angle

PLAYS (next 60 days)
Week | Sales action | Marketing action | Target person | Goal

ASSETS
Custom insight piece / business case draft / reference customer / event invite

METRICS

Meetings with buying group: target N
Opportunity: by <date>, ~<amount>

RISKS
<incumbent, budget timing, blocker, competing initiative>

## Example insight and hypothesis

Account: a national 3PL with 40 warehouses.

- What's happening: opened 6 new warehouses this year (press releases), hiring 12 operations supervisors (careers page), COO said on an earnings call that labour cost per order is the top priority.
- Value hypothesis: "Because the new warehouses are being staffed now, the 3PL could cut overtime in its first year by scheduling across sites from one view, worth about $1.2M a year at their published volumes."

## Cluster messaging for 1:few

| Cluster | Shared problem | Message | Proof |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Expanding 3PLs | New sites, new staff | Staff new sites without overtime | Peer 3PL story |
| Cold-chain logistics | Compliance and shift rules | Compliance-safe scheduling | Audit outcome |
| E-commerce fulfilment | Seasonal peaks | Scale for peak without chaos | Peak-season numbers |

Use this before the first touch on a Tier 1 account or before any first call. It produces a one-page brief that answers one question: why would this company care about us this quarter?

## Inputs

- Company name and domain.
- Your offer and ICP, so research stays relevant.
- What the CRM already knows: past conversations, open or lost deals, current customers in the same group.

## The play

### 1. Check history first
Search the CRM before the web. A lost deal from last year, an existing customer in a sister company or an unsubscribed contact changes the whole approach.

### 2. Read the primary sources, in this order
1. The company's own site: homepage claim, pricing page, careers page, newsroom.
2. Job listings: the clearest public signal of priorities, budgets and tools in use.
3. Leadership posts and interviews from the last six months.
4. Press releases, funding announcements, earnings notes for public companies.
5. Customer reviews of their product: the problems their customers complain about often become their priorities.

Stop when the brief is complete. Thirty minutes of research for a Tier 1 account, five for Tier 2.

### 3. Pick the triggers that matter
A trigger is a change that creates urgency: a new leader, funding, expansion, a hiring wave, a launch, a regulation, a bad quarter. Keep only triggers from the last 6 months and only those that connect to your offer. Read [references/trigger-library.md](references/trigger-library.md) for the trigger list with suggested angles.

### 4. Connect triggers to pains
Write each as "Because <trigger>, they probably <pain>, which we solve by <outcome>." If you cannot fill all three parts, it is trivia, not an angle.

### 5. Name the people
Economic buyer, likely champion and one alternate. Include title, tenure and anything they have said publicly about the problem.

## Output format

```
Account: <name> (<domain>)  |  Fit: Tier 1/2/3  |  CRM history: <one line>
What they do: <one sentence in plain words>
Priorities this year: <2-3 bullets, each with source>
Triggers (last 6 months): <date - event - source>
Likely pains: <2-3, each tied to a trigger or evidence>
People: <name - title - why them>
Angles:
  1. <angle> - opener idea - source
  2. ...
  3. ...
Risks: <reasons this might be a bad fit or bad timing>
```

## What good looks like

- Every angle has a dated source. A brief full of unsourced claims is worse than no brief.
- The angles are about the prospect's situation, not your features.
- The best researchers notice what is missing: no sales leader on the team page, a pricing page that changed, a product line that quietly disappeared.
- Risks are listed. A brief that only argues for outreach is a sales pitch to yourself.
- The common mistake is summarising the company's About page. That tells a rep nothing they could not guess.

## Rules

- MUST check CRM history before external research.
- MUST date and source every trigger and angle.
- NEVER treat information older than 12 months as a current trigger.
- NEVER use personal information unrelated to the person's work.

## Example prompts

- "Research northwind.com before my call on Thursday. We sell warehouse scheduling software."
- "Give me an account brief and three angles for Acme Health. Tier 1, VP Operations is the buyer."
- "Research these 10 accounts and rank them by how timely outreach would be."

references.title: Trigger library
references.markdown:
# Trigger library

Triggers ranked by how reliably they create a buying window. "Window" is how long the urgency usually lasts.

| Trigger | Where to find it | Window | Why it matters | Example angle |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| New leader in the buying role | Leadership posts, company news, profile changes | First 90 days | New leaders audit tools and want early wins | "Most new sales leaders I talk to review the outbound stack in month one..." |
| Funding round | Press releases, funding databases | 3-6 months | Budget plus pressure to grow fast | "With the Series B, the plan likely calls for pipeline to double..." |
| Hiring for a role your product supports | Careers page, job boards | While the listing is open | They are paying to solve the problem; you may be cheaper or faster | "Saw you're hiring three SDRs. Teams usually..." |
| Expansion: new region, office, product line | Newsroom, leadership posts | 3-6 months | New processes get built from scratch | "Opening in Germany means..." |
| Tool change | Job listings naming tools, review sites | 6 months | Migration projects open the door to adjacent tools | "Since you're moving to a new CRM..." |
| Regulation or compliance deadline | Industry news | Until the deadline | Fixed date, non-negotiable | "With the deadline in March..." |
| Bad results or layoffs | Earnings, news | 3 months | Efficiency pitches land; growth pitches do not | Lead with cost and time saved, gently |
| Competitor customer churn | Reviews, community threads | 1-3 months | Active pain with a named alternative | "Teams switching from the old way usually ask..." |
| Event participation | Event agendas, speaker lists | 2 weeks around the event | A natural, timely reason to talk | "Saw you're speaking at..." |

## Weak triggers to skip

- Generic awards and "best places to work" lists.
- Website redesigns with no strategic change.
- Anniversaries.
- Old funding (over 12 months) presented as news.

## Writing the trigger into an opener

Formula: **observation → implication → question**. Keep the observation factual and the implication humble.

- Weak: "Congrats on the funding! We help companies grow."
- Strong: "Saw the Series B last month and four SDR roles on your careers page. Teams in that spot usually hit a list-building bottleneck before they hit a headcount one. Is that on your radar yet?"

Use this when there are more accounts than time. It produces tiers that tell every rep how much effort each account deserves, and a score breakdown that makes the tier defensible.

## Inputs

- The account list with whatever firmographics exist.
- The ICP with must-haves, nice-to-haves and disqualifiers.
- Signals and history: intent, website visits, past opportunities, engagement, triggers.

## The play

### 1. Score fit and timing separately
Fit says whether the account could ever buy; timing says whether it might buy now. Keep them as two numbers on a 0-100 scale. Combining them too early hides great-fit accounts that are simply not ready, and they belong in nurture, not the bin.

Read [references/tiering-rubric.md](references/tiering-rubric.md) for the full rubric, the weights and the tie-break rules.

### 2. Place each account on the grid

| | Timing high (60+) | Timing low |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Fit high (70+)** | Tier 1 | Tier 2 |
| **Fit medium (50-69)** | Tier 2 | Tier 3 |
| **Fit low (under 50)** | Tier 3 or out | Out |

### 3. Cap Tier 1
Tier 1 is limited by research capacity: roughly 20 to 50 accounts per rep at a time. If the scoring puts 400 accounts in Tier 1, raise the thresholds instead of diluting the effort.

### 4. Attach effort rules
| Tier | Research | Personalization | Channels | Contacts per account |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 20-30 min account + person research | 1:1 opener per person | Email, LinkedIn, phone, video | 3-5 |
| 2 | 5 min trigger check | Segment message plus a personal line | Email and LinkedIn | 2-3 |
| 3 | None | Segment message | Email or LinkedIn | 1-2 |

### 5. Re-tier on a schedule
Timing changes weekly. Re-score monthly, and immediately when a strong signal fires (new leader, funding, high-intent page visit).

## Output format

```
account | fit score | timing score | tier | top 3 score drivers | next action
```

Plus a summary: counts per tier, Tier 1 capacity check, and accounts that moved tiers since the last run.

## What good looks like

- A rep reading the score drivers agrees with the tier more than 8 times out of 10. If they do not, the weights are wrong.
- Tier 1 fits the team's research capacity.

references.title: Tiering rubric
references.markdown:
# Tiering rubric

## Fit score (0-100)

| Component | Points | How to score |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Core ICP must-haves | 0-45 | Even split across must-haves; any miss caps fit at 49 |
| Size in the sweet spot | 0-15 | Full points in the band where win rate is highest, half in adjacent bands |
| Nice-to-haves | 0-15 | Stack match, business model detail, region |
| Reachable buying group | 0-15 | Named buyer and champion with verified channels |
| Relationship assets | 0-10 | Former customer champion now there, shared investor, warm intro path |
| Disqualifier | Fit = 0 | Overrides all |

## Timing score (0-100)

| Signal | Points | Decay |
| --- | --- | --- |
| New leader in the buying role | 30 | Halves after 90 days |
| Hiring for a role your product supports | 25 | Zero when the listing closes |
| Funding round | 20 | Halves after 120 days |
| High-intent web visits (pricing, comparison, demo pages) | 25 | Halves after 14 days |
| Engagement with your content or team | 15 | Halves after 30 days |
| Third-party intent on your category | 15 | Halves after 30 days |
| Past opportunity lost to "timing" | 15 | Peaks at the date they named |

Cap timing at 100.

## Tie-breaks inside a tier

1. Higher timing first.
2. Then accounts with an existing relationship asset.
3. Then larger potential contract value.

## Calibrating the weights

After a quarter, compare tiers with outcomes:

| Tier | Accounts | Meetings | Meeting rate | Opportunities |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 120 | 34 | 28% | 19 |
| 2 | 480 | 41 | 9% | 17 |
| 3 | 1,400 | 22 | 2% | 6 |

Healthy pattern: each tier converts at roughly 2-4x the tier below. If Tier 1 and Tier 2 convert at similar rates, the fit weights are not discriminating; look at which components the Tier 2 winners scored low on and raise those weights.

Use this when buyers ask AI assistants which tool to use and your brand is missing or described wrongly. AI answers favour sources that state facts clearly, answer the question directly and are confirmed by other sources.

## Inputs

- The category, product and the facts that define it (who it is for, pricing model, key capabilities, integrations).
- The pages that should be cited: home, product, pricing, comparisons, docs.
- The questions buyers ask (from sales calls, search and support).

## The play

### 1. Map the questions
Group buyer questions by type: "what is", "best tools for", "x vs y", "how to", "how much does", "is x good for <use case>". Prioritise commercial questions where a recommendation is made.

### 2. Audit current answers
Ask several assistants the top questions. Record whether you are mentioned, what is said, which sources are cited and what is wrong or outdated. Repeat monthly; answers change.

### 3. Rewrite pages for extraction
Read [references/aeo-checklist.md](references/aeo-checklist.md) for the page-level checklist. The core:
- Lead each section with a direct, one or two sentence answer, then the detail.
- State facts plainly and consistently across pages: what it is, who it is for, price, limits.
- Use comparison tables with clear criteria; assistants reuse tables well.
- Name entities precisely: product names, categories, integrations, use cases.
- Keep facts fresh and dated where they change.

### 4. Make it machine-readable
Organization, Product or SoftwareApplication, FAQPage and Article schema; a clean sitemap; fast, crawlable HTML (key text not hidden behind scripts); an `llms.txt` summary with links to the most important pages; and no blocking of the AI crawlers you want to be cited by.

### 5. Build corroboration
Assistants trust facts confirmed elsewhere: review sites, directories, partner pages, community answers, credible articles. Make sure third-party descriptions match your own.

## Output format

```
Question map: <question - type - priority - currently mentioned? - cited sources>
Wrong or missing facts: <...>
Page fixes: <page - change - why>
Schema and technical: <...>
Corroboration targets: <sources to update or earn>
Re-check: <date and questions to re-run>
```

## What good looks like

- One consistent fact sheet about the product, reused everywhere.
- Comparison and "best for" pages that are honest about fit; assistants pick up balanced sources.
- Progress measured by mentions and citations on the priority questions, checked monthly.
- The common mistake is writing for keywords alone, with answers buried in paragraph four of a long intro.

## Rules

- MUST keep every claim accurate and consistent across pages.
- MUST measure with repeatable question sets over time, not one-off screenshots.
- NEVER publish fake reviews, fake third-party pages or hidden text aimed at AI crawlers.
- NEVER make claims about competitors you cannot support.

## Example prompts

- "Audit how AI assistants describe us for 'best AI SDR tools' and fix our pages."
- "Rewrite our pricing page so answer engines quote it correctly."
- "Build a monthly AEO tracking sheet for our 20 most important buyer questions."

references.title: AEO page checklist
references.markdown:
# AEO page checklist

## Content

- [ ] The page's main question is answered in the first 1-2 sentences.
- [ ] Each H2 is a question or a clear topic, and its first sentence answers it.
- [ ] Facts are stated plainly: "X is a <category> for <who>. It costs <price> per <unit>."
- [ ] Product name, category and audience are used consistently with other pages.
- [ ] Comparison tables have explicit criteria and honest "best for" rows.
- [ ] Numbers carry a source or a date.
- [ ] A short FAQ answers the 5-8 most common questions in 40-80 words each.
- [ ] No important text exists only in images, tabs that need clicks, or scripts.

## Technical

- [ ] Server-rendered HTML with the main content present on load.
- [ ] Organization schema (name, logo, sameAs profiles).
- [ ] SoftwareApplication or Product schema with offers where pricing is public.
- [ ] FAQPage schema matching the visible FAQ.
- [ ] Article schema with author and dates on content pages.
- [ ] Sitemap includes the page; canonical is correct.
- [ ] `robots.txt` allows the assistants' crawlers the business wants to be cited by.
- [ ] `llms.txt` at the root lists the key pages with one-line descriptions.

## Fact sheet (keep one, reuse everywhere)

| Fact | Value | Where it appears |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One-line description | | Home, about, directories, profiles |
| Category | | |
| Best for | | |
| Not for | | |
| Pricing model and starting price | | Pricing, comparisons |
| Key capabilities (5) | | |
| Integrations | | |
| Founded, HQ, team size (if public) | | |

## Corroboration sources to check

- Review and software directory profiles.
- Integration partners' listing pages.
- Community answers and forum threads about the category.
- Articles and lists that rank for "best <category>" queries.
- The company's own social profiles and bios.

Each one should describe the product the same way as the fact sheet.

Use this for the last touch. A good break-up email respects the reader's silence, removes pressure and makes a one-line answer easy, which is why it often pulls the highest reply rate of the sequence.

## Inputs

- The thread so far.
- Stage: cold sequence, stalled deal, or a relationship you want to keep.
- What you would send if they said yes later (a checklist, a story, a short demo).

## The play

### 1. Choose the version
| Version | Use when | Tone |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cold close | No reply after 3-4 cold touches | Light, brief, easy out |
| Deal close | Engaged prospect went silent for 3+ weeks | Honest, direct, helpful |
| Door open | Good fit, wrong time | Warm, with a future trigger |

### 2. Keep the structure tight
1. Say this is the last note (without drama).
2. Offer one easy reply: a single word, or a multiple-choice.
3. Leave something useful or a reason to come back later.
4. Wish them well, sincerely.

25-50 words for cold; up to 80 for deals.

### 3. Set the next step
After the break-up, contacts move to a nurture: no sales email for 90 days unless they reply or a strong new signal fires.

## Examples

**Cold close**

> Hi Maya, I will stop here so I don't clutter your inbox. If faster month-end closes become a priority, reply "close" and I will send the checklist Contoso used. Good luck with quarter end.

**Deal close**

> Hi Tom, I have not heard back since the proposal, so I am going to assume this has moved down the list and close it on my side. If that is wrong, a one-line reply is all it takes to pick up where we left off. Either way, thank you for the time your team gave us.

**Door open**

> Hi Ana, sounds like timing is the issue rather than fit. I will check back in Q3 when you mentioned the budget cycle starts. In the meantime, here is the rollout plan other 10-location groups used, in case it is useful.

## What good looks like

- No guilt, no passive aggression, no "I guess you're not interested".
- A real one-word reply option.
- The common mistake is the sarcastic break-up ("Have you been eaten by a bear?"). It sometimes gets replies but costs goodwill with exactly the people you want to sell to later.

## Rules

- MUST make it clear this is the last email in the sequence.
- MUST stop all sequence emails afterwards unless they reply.
- NEVER use sarcasm, guilt or fake scarcity.
- NEVER claim you are "closing their file" in a way that sounds like a threat.

## Example prompts

- "Write the final email for our 4-step cold sequence to CFOs."
- "This deal went quiet for a month after the demo. Write a break-up email."
- "Write a door-open email for a prospect who said maybe next year."

Use this before writing to a role you have not sold to before, or when outreach reads like it was written for nobody in particular. It produces one persona card per role that changes what a rep writes.

## Inputs

- The job titles in the buying committee, or the deal type so you can propose them.
- Raw evidence: call recordings or notes, won-deal emails, support tickets, reviews, job listings for the role.
- The ICP and the product's core job.

## The play

### 1. Separate the roles
A deal usually has four: the **economic buyer** who signs, the **champion** who feels the pain and pushes, **users** who live in the tool, and the **blocker** (security, finance, IT, legal) who can stop it. Build a card per role. One blended persona produces messages that fit no one.

### 2. Start from what they are measured on
The fastest route to relevance is the number on their scorecard. A VP Sales is measured on bookings and forecast accuracy; a RevOps lead on data quality and tool cost; a founder on runway and growth rate. Pains connect to these numbers or they do not matter.

### 3. Use their words
Mine the evidence for exact phrases. Job listings are the most underrated source: they spell out the problems the company is paying to fix and the tools in use.

### 4. Map objections and proof
For each role, list the top three objections and the proof that answers each one: a customer story, a number, a demo moment, a security document.

### 5. Find the angle
One sentence per role: the reason this person would take a meeting this quarter.

## Persona card format

```
Role: <title variants>            Type: economic buyer | champion | user | blocker
Measured on: <2-3 metrics>
Goals this year: <2-3>
Pains (their words): <3 quotes or close paraphrases, with source>
Triggers: <events that make the pain urgent>
Objections → proof: <3 pairs>
Trusted sources: <communities, newsletters, peers, analysts>
Angle: <one sentence>
Do not say: <phrases that make them tune out>
```

Read [references/persona-examples.md](references/persona-examples.md) for two complete cards and the most common do-not-say phrases by role.

## What good looks like

- A rep reading the card can write a different first line for a VP Sales and a RevOps manager at the same company.
- Pains are quoted or traceable, not imagined. "Struggles with efficiency" is a sign the evidence step was skipped.
- The blocker has a card. Deals die in security review far more often than in the first call.

Use this before writing to a role you have not sold to before, or when outreach reads like it was written for nobody in particular. It produces one persona card per role that changes what a rep writes.

Inputs

  • The job titles in the buying committee, or the deal type so you can propose them.
  • Raw evidence: call recordings or notes, won-deal emails, support tickets, reviews, job listings for the role.
  • The ICP and the product's core job.

The play

1. Separate the roles

A deal usually has four: the economic buyer who signs, the champion who feels the pain and pushes, users who live in the tool, and the blocker (security, finance, IT, legal) who can stop it. Build a card per role. One blended persona produces messages that fit no one.

The fastest route to relevance is the number on their scorecard. A VP Sales is measured on bookings and forecast accuracy; a RevOps lead on data quality and tool cost; a founder on runway and growth rate. Pains connect to these numbers or they do not matter.

4. Map objections and proof

For each role, list the top three objections and the proof that answers each one: a customer story, a number, a demo moment, a security document.

5. Find the angle

One sentence per role: the reason this person would take a meeting this quarter.

references.title: Persona examples
references.markdown:
# Persona examples

## Champion: Head of Sales Development (product: outbound automation)

```
Role: Head of SDR, SDR Manager, Director of Sales Development
Type: champion
Measured on: meetings held per rep, pipeline created, ramp time
Goals this year: hit meeting targets with a flat headcount; ramp new reps in under 60 days
Pains (their words):
  - "My reps spend half the day building lists instead of talking to people." (call notes)
  - "Every new rep writes their own sequences and half of them are bad." (call notes)
  - "We burned two domains last quarter." (community thread)
Triggers: new quarterly target, a rep resignation, a domain landing in spam, new VP Sales
Objections → proof:
  - "AI emails sound robotic" → side-by-side of a sourced, personalised draft
  - "My reps will resist it" → rep-level time saved per week from a similar team
  - "We already have a sequencer" → what it does not do: research and reply drafting
Trusted sources: sales development communities, peer SDR leaders, practitioner newsletters
Angle: more held meetings per rep without adding headcount
Do not say: "replace your SDRs", "10x", "set it and forget it"
```

## Blocker: Head of IT or Security (any SaaS that touches customer data)

```
Role: IT Manager, Head of Security, CISO at larger accounts
Type: blocker
Measured on: incidents, audit findings, vendor count, access reviews passed
Goals this year: pass the next audit; reduce shadow IT
Pains (their words):
  - "Sales buys tools and tells us after the contract is signed."
  - "I need to know where the data goes and who can see it."
Triggers: audit cycle, a vendor breach in the news, a new compliance requirement
Objections → proof:
  - "Where is data stored?" → data-flow diagram and sub-processor list
  - "Do you train on our data?" → written data-use policy
  - "SSO and access control?" → admin screenshots and role list
Trusted sources: security questionnaires, peer CISOs, compliance frameworks
Angle: a vendor review that takes one meeting, not six weeks
Do not say: "it is totally secure", "nobody has ever asked"
```

## Common do-not-say phrases by role

| Role | Tunes out at |
| --- | --- |
| Founders and CEOs | "Quick question", "I'd love to pick your brain", long intros about you |
| VP Sales | "Increase productivity" without a number, "AI-powered" as the lead |
| RevOps | "Seamless integration" without naming the objects and fields |
| Finance | "Pays for itself" without the maths |
| Marketing leaders | "Generate more leads" (they are measured on pipeline, not leads) |
| Engineers and IT | Superlatives of any kind |

  category: prospecting

  author: prosyo

  keywords: "buying committee map, stakeholder mapping sales, multithreading deals, claude stakeholder map skill, decision makers b2b"
  inputs: "Account or deal, Known contacts, Deal size and product"

---

Use this whenever a deal depends on one person. Single-threaded deals close far less often than deals with three or more engaged contacts, and they die quietly when the one contact changes jobs or goes quiet.

## Inputs

- The account or deal, its size and stage.
- Contacts already engaged and what each has said.
- The product and the departments it touches.

## The play

### 1. List the roles the deal needs
| Role | Question they answer | Typical titles |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Economic buyer | Is it worth the money? | VP, C-level, budget owner |
| Champion | Will this make my life and my team better? | Manager or director who feels the pain |
| Technical evaluator | Will it work with what we have? | IT, engineering, operations, RevOps |
| Users | Will I actually use it? | Individual contributors |
| Blockers | Is it safe and compliant? | Security, legal, procurement, finance |
| Influencers | What do I recommend? | Peers, advisors, adjacent team leads |

Deal size sets how many roles show up: under $10k often 1-2 people; $10-50k usually 3-5; above $100k usually 6-10.

### 2. Name the people
For each role, find the most likely person at the account. Mark each as confirmed (they told you or you met them) or inferred (from the org chart or titles).

### 3. Score each contact
Engagement (none, aware, engaged, active) and sentiment (supporter, neutral, sceptic, unknown). An unknown blocker is the most dangerous cell on the map.

### 4. Plan the threads
For each gap, decide who reaches out (rep, manager, executive sponsor, solutions engineer), through which route (champion introduction is best, then direct), and what that person needs to hear in their own language.

### 5. Arm the champion
Give the champion the material they need to sell internally: a one-paragraph business case, the security pack, a short answer to the most likely objection from each other role.

## Output format

```
Deal: <account> - <size> - <stage>
Committee:
  role | name | title | confirmed/inferred | engagement | sentiment | what they need
Coverage: <roles engaged / roles needed>  Risk: <single-threaded? unknown blocker?>
Plan: <next 3 actions with owner and date>
Champion kit: <items to send>
```

## What good looks like

- At least three engaged contacts before a deal is called "commit".
- The blocker is identified before the proposal, not after.
- Outreach to new contacts goes through the champion when possible, so it reads as collaboration rather than going around them.
- The common mistake is mapping titles without talking to anyone: a map full of inferred names gives false comfort.

## Rules

- MUST mark each person as confirmed or inferred.
- MUST flag any deal with a single engaged contact as at risk.
- NEVER contact a new stakeholder in a way that undermines the champion without discussing it with them first.

## Example prompts

- "Map the buying committee for our $80k deal with Contoso. I only talk to the IT manager."
- "Who else should I bring into this deal, and how?"
- "Build a multi-threading plan for my top 5 deals."

skills.title: Buying signal scoring
skills.description: Use this skill when you track buying signals and need to decide which ones deserve outreach today: "which accounts are in market", "prioritise these signals", "build a signal-based selling system". Catalogues the signals that matter for your offer (hiring, funding, leadership changes, intent, website visits, engagement, tech changes), scores them on strength and freshness, stacks multiple signals per account, and outputs a daily ranked action list with the play to run for each. The core of signal-based outbound.

  category: signals
  tags: "SDR, Sales, RevOps, Founders"
  author: prosyo
  version: "1.0.0"
  keywords: "buying signals, signal based selling, intent signals scoring, claude buying signals skill, in-market accounts"
  inputs: "Signal feed or list of events, ICP and account tiers, Your offer"
  outputs: "Signal catalogue with weights, Daily ranked action list, Play per signal"
---

Use this to turn a noisy stream of events into a short list of accounts to contact today, with a reason and a play for each.

## Inputs

- The signals available: job listings, leadership changes, funding, web visits, content engagement, third-party intent, technology changes, product usage for existing users.
- The ICP and account tiers.
- The offer, so each signal can be tied to a reason to talk.

## The play

### 1. Build the signal catalogue
List every signal you can detect. For each, write the "so what": why this event makes your offer more relevant now. Signals without a clear "so what" are noise, however easy they are to collect.

### 2. Weight by strength and freshness
Strength reflects how often the signal precedes a real opportunity. Freshness reflects how fast it decays. Read [references/signal-weights.md](references/signal-weights.md) for the starter weights, decay curves and the stacking rules.

### 3. Stack signals per account
One signal is a hint; two or three on the same account in the same month is a pattern. Score = sum of decayed signal weights × fit multiplier (Tier 1: 1.0, Tier 2: 0.7, Tier 3: 0.4). Accounts outside the ICP get no multiplier and do not make the list, however loud their signals.

### 4. Pick the play
Each signal type maps to a play: who to contact, the angle, the channel and the timing. A new VP gets a "first 90 days" angle; a pricing-page visit gets a fast, low-pressure helpful touch; a hiring wave gets a "before your new team starts" angle.

### 5. Produce the daily list
Rank by score, cap at the team's capacity (typically 15-30 signal-led touches per rep per day), and include the evidence so reps can write in seconds.

## Output format

```
rank | account | score | signals (type - date - source) | contact | play | suggested opener
```

Plus: signals that fired on accounts outside the ICP (for review), and signals that decayed without action this week.

## What good looks like

- Every row has evidence a rep can check in one click.
- The list is short enough to finish. A 300-row "hot list" is a cold list.
- Plays reference the situation, never the surveillance: "teams that just raised often..." not "I saw you were on our pricing page".
- Stacked signals beat single loud ones. One webinar attendance is weaker than a new VP plus two relevant job listings.
- The common mistake is treating every signal as equal and blasting the same template the moment anything fires.

## Rules

- MUST apply the ICP filter before ranking.
- MUST decay signals over time.
- NEVER reveal in outreach that you tracked someone's website visit or profile view.
- NEVER contact the same person on more than one signal in the same week.

## Example prompts

- "Here are this week's signals across our 800 target accounts. Who should we contact today?"
- "Design a signal catalogue and weights for our HR software."
- "Turn these funding and hiring alerts into a ranked list with openers."

references.title: Signal weights and stacking
references.markdown:
# Signal weights and stacking

## Starter weights

Calibrate after one quarter by comparing which signals preceded real opportunities.

| Signal | Weight | Half-life | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Demo or pricing form started but not finished | 40 | 3 days | Highest intent; human follow-up same day |
| Pricing or comparison page visits (company-level) | 30 | 7 days | Use as timing only, never mention it |
| Former champion joined a new company | 35 | 60 days | Strongest warm signal in B2B |
| New leader in buying role | 30 | 45 days | |
| Hiring for a role the product supports | 25 | Until closed | Two or more listings: +10 |
| Funding round | 20 | 60 days | Larger rounds raise weight only if the plan names your function |
| Engaged with your post or content | 15 | 14 days | Comment > like |
| Third-party category intent | 15 | 14 days | Noisy; treat as tie-breaker |
| Technology added or removed | 15 | 60 days | Strong if it is a complement or a competitor |
| Event attendance or speaking | 10 | 14 days | |
| Expansion news: office, region, product | 15 | 60 days | |
| Negative news: layoffs, bad quarter | 10 | 30 days | Changes the angle to efficiency |

Decay: weight × 0.5^(days since signal ÷ half-life).

## Stacking rules

- Same signal type twice in a week counts once.
- Two different signal types in 30 days: add a 1.2x bonus.
- Three or more types in 30 days: 1.5x bonus and a Tier 1 treatment regardless of the account's static tier.

## Play map

| Signal | Who | Angle | Channel | Timing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| New leader | The leader | First-90-days priorities | LinkedIn then email | Days 14-45 in seat |
| Hiring wave | Hiring manager | Help the new team ramp | Email | Within 7 days of the listing |
| Funding | Founder or functional VP | The growth plan's bottleneck | Email | Weeks 2-6 after news |
| Former champion moved | The champion | Reconnect, no pitch | LinkedIn message | Days 30-60 in new job |
| High-intent page visits | Likely buyer at the account | Helpful resource for the problem | Email | Within 24 hours |
| Content engagement | The person | Continue the conversation | LinkedIn | Within 48 hours |

## Calibration table

| Signal | Accounts with signal | Opportunities in 90 days | Rate | Keep weight? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

Raise the weight of any signal converting at 2x the average, cut any converting below the average.

  inputs: "Call transcript or notes, Call type and goal, Rep level"
  outputs: "Scorecard, Quoted moments, One focus skill, Practice drill"

Use this after calls worth learning from: a first call, a lost deal, a new rep's first week. Coaching works when it is specific, quoted and focused on one thing at a time.

## Inputs

- The transcript (or detailed notes).
- Call type (cold call, discovery, demo, negotiation) and its goal.
- The rep's experience level.

## The play

### 1. Measure the basics
Talk ratio (rep vs buyer), number of questions asked, longest rep monologue, whether a next step was booked. Talk ratio over 60% on a discovery call is a red flag on its own.

### 2. Score the dimensions (1-4)
| Dimension | What 4 looks like |
| --- | --- |
| Opening | Clear agenda, buyer adds to it, permission to ask questions |
| Discovery | Layered questions to impact and priority; follow-ups on answers |
| Listening | Paraphrases, uses the buyer's words, does not interrupt |
| Value | Connects the product to the buyer's stated problem, with proof |
| Objections | Clarifies before answering; calm; checks the answer landed |
| Next step | Specific, dated, agreed on the call, with the right people |

Read [references/scorecard-rubric.md](references/scorecard-rubric.md) for the full rubric per call type and example quotes for each score.

### 3. Quote the moments
Two strengths and two misses, each with the exact quote and timestamp, and what a better line would have been.

### 4. Pick one focus
The single skill that would most change results on the next five calls. Usually the earliest weak stage: weak discovery causes weak value and weak next steps.

### 5. Give a drill
A 10-15 minute exercise for the focus skill: rewrite three questions, a role-play of the missed moment, or listen to a great call and note how the top rep handled the same moment.

## Output format

```
Call: <type> | <rep> | <date>   Goal: <...>   Outcome: <next step or not>
Talk ratio: x% | Questions: N | Longest monologue: N min
Scores: Opening x | Discovery x | Listening x | Value x | Objections x | Next step x
Strengths: <quote - why it worked> x2
Misses: <quote - better line> x2
Focus for next calls: <one skill>
Drill: <exercise>
```

## What good looks like

- Feedback quotes the call; no "be more consultative" without an example.
- One focus, not ten notes.
- Praise is as specific as criticism.
- The common mistake is scoring everything and changing nothing: a manager who gives seven pieces of feedback gets none of them applied.

## Rules

- MUST quote the call for every strength and miss.
- MUST pick one focus skill.
- MUST respect call-recording consent and keep transcripts private to the rep and their manager.
- NEVER share a rep's scores publicly or compare reps by name in team settings.

## Example prompts

- "Score this discovery call transcript and give me one thing to work on."
- "Build a call scorecard our 4 managers can use consistently."
- "Review my cold calls from today; I keep losing them at 'send me an email'."

references.title: Call scorecard rubric
references.markdown:
# Call scorecard rubric

## Discovery call

| Dimension | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Opening | Jumps in, no agenda | States agenda | Agenda + buyer's goals asked | Agenda, buyer adds to it, permission to dig in |
| Discovery | Few or closed questions | Situation questions only | Reaches problem and some impact | Reaches impact, priority and decision process with follow-ups |
| Listening | Interrupts, talks 70%+ | Talks 55-70% | Talks 40-55%, some paraphrasing | Talks under 40%, uses the buyer's words back |
| Value | Feature tour | Generic benefits | Ties one feature to stated pain | Ties to pain + impact with matching proof |
| Objections | Argues or ignores | Answers without clarifying | Clarifies, then answers | Clarifies, answers, checks it landed |
| Next step | None or vague | "I'll send info" | Next step agreed, no date | Dated, in calendar, right people invited |

## Cold call

| Dimension | 4 looks like |
| --- | --- |
| Opener | Honest, permission-based, under 15 seconds |
| Reason | Problem stated in buyer terms with a peer reference, ends in a question |
| Engagement | Asks a follow-up question on their answer |
| Brush-off | Acknowledges, one question, respects the answer |
| Ask | Specific time options or a referral; clear outcome either way |

## Example quotes by score (discovery)

- Discovery 1: "So do you use a scheduling tool?" (closed, leads nowhere)
- Discovery 4: "You said Mondays are chaos. What happens to the rest of the week when Monday goes wrong? ... Roughly how many hours does that cost the team?"
- Listening 4: "So if I heard you right, it's not the software, it's that nobody owns cross-site cover. Is that fair?"
- Next step 2: "I'll send over some info and we can go from there."
- Next step 4: "Let's do Thursday at 10 with you and Dev; I'll send the invite now and bring the cross-site cover example."

## Focus skill picker

If several dimensions score low, coach the earliest in the call first: opening → discovery → listening → value → objections → next step. Improvements early in the call lift the later scores on their own.

Use this weekly or at the end of a campaign. It answers three questions: what is working, where does it break, and what do we change next.

## Inputs

- Per campaign: contacts, sent, delivered or bounced, replies, positive replies, meetings booked and held, by step, segment, sender and channel.
- Opportunities and pipeline created from those meetings.
- The period.

## The play

### 1. Build the funnel
Contacts → delivered → replied → positive → booked → held → opportunity. Calculate each conversion. Skip open rates as a decision metric; open tracking is unreliable and often turned off for deliverability.

### 2. Benchmark
Read [references/outbound-benchmarks.md](references/outbound-benchmarks.md) for typical ranges by channel and what each gap usually means. Benchmarks are a sanity check, not a target; your own trend matters more.

### 3. Find the break
The first stage below benchmark is the problem to fix; improving later stages first is wasted effort.

| Break | Usually means | Look at |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bounces | List quality | Source, verification, catch-alls |
| Low replies, few negatives | Not seen, or not relevant | Deliverability by sender; targeting; first line |
| Replies, few positive | Message or offer mismatch | Angle, persona, ask |
| Positive, few booked | Slow or weak reply handling | Time to respond, booking flow |
| Booked, few held | Weak qualification or reminders | No-show rate, lead time |
| Held, few opportunities | Wrong ICP or poor discovery | Fit of meetings, discovery quality |

### 4. Slice it
By step (which email gets the replies), segment (which persona or industry), sender (deliverability or skill), channel. Small slices need samples of 100+ contacts before conclusions.

### 5. Recommend the next test
One test at a time on the broken stage, with a hypothesis and a success threshold.

## Output format

```
Period: | Campaigns: | Contacts:
Funnel (all): contacts → delivered x% → replied x% → positive x% → booked x% → held x% → opps
Best / worst campaign: <name - why>
The break: <stage - evidence - likely cause>
Slices worth noting: <step, segment, sender findings with sample sizes>
Next test: <hypothesis - change - metric - threshold - sample>
Stop / scale: <campaigns to pause, campaigns to give more volume>
```

## What good looks like

- Diagnosis follows the funnel order.
- Every conclusion states its sample size.
- The report ends in one or two decisions, not twenty observations.
- The common mistake is optimising subject lines when a third of the emails bounce or land in spam.

## Rules

- MUST report sample sizes and flag anything under 100 contacts as directional.
- MUST check deliverability by sender before judging copy.
- NEVER call a test winner on fewer than 200 contacts per variant.

## Example prompts

- "Here's last month's export for 6 campaigns. What's working and what should we change?"
- "Our reply rate halved this month. Find out why."
- "Build a weekly outbound report template for our SDR team."

references.title: Outbound benchmarks
references.markdown:
# Outbound benchmarks

Typical ranges for well-run B2B outbound to a targeted list. They vary by market, deal size and offer; use them to spot outliers, then track your own trend.

## Cold email

| Metric | Weak | Typical | Strong |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bounce rate | > 3% | 1-2% | < 1% |
| Reply rate (any) | < 2% | 3-6% | 8%+ |
| Positive reply rate (of contacts) | < 0.5% | 1-2% | 3%+ |
| Positive share of replies | < 25% | 30-45% | 50%+ |
| Meetings per 100 contacts | < 0.5 | 0.8-1.5 | 2+ |
| Spam complaint rate | > 0.3% | < 0.1% | ~0 |

## LinkedIn

| Metric | Weak | Typical | Strong |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Acceptance rate | < 20% | 25-40% | 45%+ |
| Reply rate (of accepted) | < 8% | 10-20% | 25%+ |
| Meetings per 100 invitations | < 1 | 1-3 | 4+ |

## Calls

| Metric | Typical |
| --- | --- |
| Connect rate (dials to conversations) | 3-10%, higher with good numbers |
| Meetings per conversation | 10-20% |

## Meetings to pipeline

| Metric | Weak | Typical | Strong |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Show rate | < 70% | 75-85% | 90%+ |
| Held meeting to opportunity | < 30% | 35-50% | 60%+ |

## By step (cold email)

A healthy 4-step sequence usually gets 40-60% of its replies from step 1, 15-25% from step 2, 10-20% from step 3 and 10-15% from the break-up email. If step 1 gets almost none, the first email or deliverability is broken; if the break-up gets the most, earlier steps are too pitchy.

## Sample size guide

| Contacts per slice | How to treat results |
| --- | --- |
| < 100 | Anecdote |
| 100-300 | Directional |
| 500-1,000 | Decision-grade for big differences (2x) at typical reply rates |
| 2,000+ | Decision-grade for smaller differences (1.5x) |

Use this when a customer has a result worth sharing. The best case studies read like a story a peer would tell, with the buyer's doubts left in.

## Inputs

- Interview transcript or notes with the customer (or run the guide below).
- Results data: before and after numbers, time frames.
- What the customer has approved for publication: name, logo, quotes, numbers.

## The play

### 1. Interview for the story, not the praise
Ask:
- What was happening before? What did it cost you?
- What made you look for a change then?
- What else did you consider? What almost stopped you?
- How did the rollout actually go, including the bumps?
- What changed, in numbers, and how do you measure it?
- What would you tell a peer considering it?

### 2. Structure it
1. **Headline**: the result, with the number. "How Northwind filled 15% more chairs in 90 days."
2. **Snapshot**: company, size, use case, top 3 results.
3. **Before**: the situation and its cost, in their words.
4. **Trigger and decision**: why now, what they compared, why they chose.
5. **Rollout**: what it took, honestly.
6. **Results**: numbers with time frames and how they were measured.
7. **What's next**.

### 3. Use quotes well
Two to four quotes, each doing a job: the pain, the decision, the result. Edit for length, never for meaning, and get approval on the final wording.

### 4. Make the versions
- Website: 600-900 words with the structure above.
- Sales one-pager: snapshot, before and after, three results, one quote.
- Cold email paragraph: one sentence of before, one of after.
- LinkedIn post: the story in 150 words with the turning point.

## What good looks like

- The headline number is specific, time-bound and approved.
- The "before" is vivid enough that a prospect recognises themselves.
- Doubts and bumps are included; they make the result credible.
- The common mistake is a page of praise ("They're a great partner!") with no numbers and no story.

## Rules

- MUST get customer approval for name, quotes and numbers before publishing.
- MUST state how and over what period results were measured.
- NEVER round up results or combine customers into one story.
- NEVER publish an anonymised story with details that identify the customer anyway.

## Example prompts

- "Turn this interview transcript with Northwind into a case study and a one-pager."
- "Write interview questions for a customer who cut onboarding time by half."
- "Make a cold email paragraph and a LinkedIn post from our Contoso case study."

Use this when pipeline is thin or each quarter. Lost deals already know you, already have the problem and often lost on timing; reopening them costs far less than finding new ones.

## Inputs

- Closed-lost deals from the last 3-24 months: reason, stage lost, contacts, notes, competitor chosen.
- What changed on your side since: product releases, new pricing or packages, new proof.
- Current triggers at those accounts: new leaders, funding, hiring, the competitor's contract term ending.

## The play

### 1. Filter by reason and timing
| Lost reason | Reopen when | Angle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timing / no priority | 3-6 months later, or a trigger fires | "Is it a priority now?" |
| Budget | New fiscal year or funding | New budget, phasing options |
| Chose a competitor | 9-12 months later, before their renewal | Check-in on how it's going |
| Product gap | When the gap ships | "You asked for X; it's live" |
| No decision / went dark | 3-4 months later | New proof, fresh angle |
| Bad fit | Only if their situation changed | Usually leave it |

### 2. Score each deal
Priority = how far it got (later stage = higher) + new trigger present + the lost reason has been resolved + contacts still in role.

### 3. Lead with what changed
The message must answer "why talk again now?". Something changed: their situation (new leader, growth), your product (the missing feature), or the market (a new requirement).

### 4. Pick the contact
The original champion if still there; if they left, the new person in the role (and run a job-change play on the champion).

### 5. Write short and honest
> Hi Priya, when we spoke in March, multi-entity support was the deal-breaker. It went live last month, and Contoso is running four entities on it. Worth a fresh look, or has the team moved on?

## What good looks like

- Every message names a specific change.
- Deals lost to a competitor are approached near the end of the competitor's likely contract term, not a month after signing.
- The common mistake is re-sending the original pitch with "circling back" on top, which reminds the buyer why they said no.

## Rules

- MUST name what changed in every reactivation message.
- MUST check contacts are still in role and have not opted out.
- NEVER disparage the competitor they chose.
- NEVER misstate the reason they gave for saying no.

## Example prompts

- "Here are 120 closed-lost deals from the last 18 months. Which should we reopen and with what?"
- "We just shipped SSO. Write messages to every deal we lost because of it."
- "Plan a quarterly closed-lost reactivation play."

Use this before a calling block. It produces a talk track that sounds like a person, not a reading, and that gets to a decision (meeting or no) in under three minutes.

## Inputs

- Persona and the problem.
- Offer and one strong proof point.
- Trigger or prior touch (an email they may have seen).

## The play

### 1. Opener: honest and short
Name yourself, acknowledge the interruption, give the reason in one sentence, ask for 30 seconds.

> "Hi Maya, it's Sam from Acme. This is a cold call, so feel free to hang up, but can I tell you why I called and you decide if it's worth a minute?"

Permission-based openers convert better than pretending the call is expected.

### 2. Problem statement: the reason
One or two sentences about a problem people in their role usually have, with a peer reference. End with a question.

> "I work with finance leads at companies your size. Most tell me close takes 8 to 10 days because approvals sit in inboxes the last week of the month. Is that true for you, or have you solved it?"

### 3. Discovery: two or three questions
Ask, listen, follow the answer. Good questions are about their current process and its cost: "How long does close take today?", "Where does it get stuck?", "What happens when it runs late?"

### 4. The ask
If there is a problem: "Contoso was at 9 days and now closes in 4. Worth 20 minutes next week to see if the same thing would work for you? Tuesday or Thursday?"
If there is no problem: thank them, ask who else might feel it, and leave.

### 5. Brush-offs
Read [references/call-objections.md](references/call-objections.md) for responses to the ten most common brush-offs. The principle: acknowledge, ask one question, then respect the answer.

## One-page call card

```
Opener: <permission line>
Reason: <problem + peer>  →  "Is that true for you?"
Questions: 1. <current process>  2. <where it breaks>  3. <cost of it>
Proof: <one line>
Ask: <20 minutes, two time options>
If no: "Who else on your team deals with <problem>?"
```

## What good looks like

- The rep speaks less than 50% of the call.
- A clear outcome every time: meeting, referral, follow-up date, or a no.
- The common mistake is the pitch dump: 90 seconds of features before the prospect has said a word.

## Rules

- MUST say who you are and that it is a sales call when asked.
- MUST respect do-not-call lists and local calling rules and hours.
- NEVER pretend to know the prospect or reference a conversation that did not happen.
- NEVER keep pushing after a clear no.

## Example prompts

- "Write a cold call script for IT directors at hospitals. We sell device management."
- "Prep me for 40 calls tomorrow to people who were sent our email last week."
- "Give me responses to 'just send me an email' and 'we're all set'."

references.title: Cold call brush-offs
references.markdown:
# Cold call brush-offs

Pattern: **acknowledge → one question → respect the answer**.

| Brush-off | Response |
| --- | --- |
| "Just send me an email." | "Happy to. So I send something useful rather than a brochure, is <problem> actually something you're dealing with?" |
| "We're all set." / "We already have something." | "Good to hear. Out of curiosity, how long does <outcome> take with what you have today?" |
| "Not interested." | "Fair enough. Is that because <problem> isn't an issue, or just not a priority right now?" |
| "I'm busy right now." | "Understood. Is there a better 2 minutes later this week, or should I not call back?" |
| "How did you get my number?" | Answer honestly with the source type (a business contact database, the company website), and offer to remove it. |
| "What's this about?" (sceptical) | Give the reason in one sentence and ask the problem question. |
| "We don't have budget." | "Makes sense. When does planning for next year start? I'd rather be useful then than pushy now." |
| "Talk to <someone else>." | "Thanks. What should I know about how <name> thinks about this before I call?" |
| "Call me next quarter." | "Will do. What changes next quarter that makes it a better time?" Then book the callback date. |
| "Is this a sales call?" | "Yes, it is. Can I take 30 seconds to say why, and you decide?" |

## Voicemail after a no-answer

Under 20 seconds: name, company, one-line reason tied to the email, "I'll send you a note too", number said twice slowly. Expect few callbacks; the voicemail's job is to make the next email familiar.

## Practice drill (15 minutes)

1. Read the opener aloud five times until it sounds like you.
2. Partner plays the prospect with a random brush-off from the table; respond, then switch.
3. Record one full role-play and listen for: talk ratio, filler words, whether the ask came with two time options.

Use this to build a whole campaign rather than one email. It produces a sequence where each step has its own angle, so follow-ups add value instead of saying "just bumping this".

## Inputs

- Segment, persona and the problem the campaign is about.
- Approved proof: customer stories, numbers, assets you can share.
- Goal: meetings, replies to a question, sign-ups.

## The play

### 1. Set the shape
The default for cold B2B is 4 emails over about 14-18 days:

| Step | Day | Angle | Length |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0 | Observation → problem → proof → ask | 50-90 words |
| 2 | 3 | New angle: a different pain or a sharper insight | 40-70 words, same thread |
| 3 | 7-8 | Proof: a short customer story or a useful asset | 60-90 words, new thread |
| 4 | 14-16 | Close the loop: a polite final note, easy out | 25-50 words |

Add LinkedIn or phone steps between emails when the channel fits the persona; the multichannel cadence covers that.

### 2. Give each step one job
No step repeats the previous one. Every follow-up must stand alone: many people only ever see one of the emails. Read [references/sequence-example.md](references/sequence-example.md) for a full annotated 4-step example and step-by-step variations.

### 3. Thread deliberately
Step 2 replies in the same thread (it reads as a natural follow-up). Step 3 starts a new thread with a new subject, which gives a second chance at the inbox. Step 4 can go either way.

### 4. Define exits
People leave the sequence when they reply (any reply, including out-of-office with a return date: pause, not stop), book, bounce, opt out, or when anyone at the same account books a meeting.

### 5. Set the scorecard
Judge after 150-300 contacts per variant:

| Metric | Healthy | Action if below |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bounce rate | under 2% | Stop; clean the list |
| Reply rate | 5%+ | Rework angle or targeting |
| Positive reply rate | 1.5-3%+ | Rework offer and ask |
| Meetings per 100 contacts | 1+ | Check reply handling speed |

## What good looks like

- Step 3 could be someone's first email and still make sense.
- No "just following up", "bumping this to the top", or "did you see my last email".
- The final email is gracious and gets replies in its own right: "not a priority" answers are useful data.
- The common mistake is seven emails with the same pitch reworded; volume of touches without new value burns the list.

## Rules

- MUST give every step a distinct angle.
- MUST stop the sequence on reply, booking, bounce or opt-out.
- MUST pause, not continue, when an out-of-office names a return date.
- NEVER send more than 5 cold emails to one person in a sequence.
- NEVER guilt-trip in follow-ups.

## Example prompts

- "Write a 4-step sequence for Heads of Finance at 200-1,000 person SaaS companies. Problem: month-end close takes too long."
- "Turn this single cold email into a full sequence."
- "Our sequence gets replies on step 1 only. Rewrite steps 2-4."

references.title: Annotated 4-step sequence
references.markdown:
# Annotated 4-step sequence

Segment: Heads of Finance at 200-1,000 person SaaS companies. Problem: month-end close takes too long. Proof: Contoso closes in 4 days instead of 9 (approved).

## Step 1 (day 0)

> Subject: month-end close
>
> Hi Maya, finance teams at Lumen's size usually close in 8-10 days, and most of that time goes to chasing approvals and reconciling spreadsheets.
>
> Contoso's team was at 9 days last year. They now close in 4, mostly by automating the reconciliations that used to sit with two analysts.
>
> Is a faster close on your list this year?

Job: name the problem and prove it is solvable. 60 words.

## Step 2 (day 3, same thread)

> Hi Maya, one more angle: the slow part is rarely the accounting itself. It is the 30-40 approvals that wait in inboxes over the last week of the month.
>
> If that sounds familiar, I can send the checklist Contoso used to cut them in half.

Job: a sharper insight plus a give. 48 words.

## Step 3 (day 8, new thread)

> Subject: how contoso closes in 4 days
>
> Hi Maya, a short story in case it is useful. Contoso's controller, Priya, had two analysts spending the last week of every month matching bank lines to invoices. They automated the matching, moved approvals into one queue and set a day-3 cut-off.
>
> Result: a 4-day close and one analyst moved to forecasting. Happy to share what they changed first.

Job: proof as a story; works as a standalone first email. 70 words.

## Step 4 (day 15, same thread as step 3)

> Hi Maya, I will stop here. If faster closes become a priority later, just reply "close" and I will send the Contoso checklist. Either way, good luck with quarter end.

Job: graceful exit, one-word reply option. 35 words.

## Variations by situation

| Situation | Change |
| --- | --- |
| Very senior persona (C-level) | 3 steps, each under 60 words, longer gaps (day 0, 5, 12) |
| Strong trigger (new leader, funding) | Step 1 leads with the trigger; step 2 offers a stage-specific asset |
| Technical persona | Step 2 becomes a concrete how-it-works detail, no adjectives |
| Agency or services offer | Step 3 is a mini case study with a screenshot offer (not an attachment) |
| Low volume, Tier 1 | Step 1 fully 1:1; steps 2-4 semi-personal |

## Out-of-office handling

- Return date given: pause the sequence until 2 business days after the return, then resume at the next step.
- "No longer with the company": stop, mark the contact, and look for the replacement.
- Referral in the auto-reply ("contact Sam instead"): start Sam on step 1 with a line naming the referral.

description: "Use this skill when you need to write a B2B cold email that gets replies: \"write a cold email to a VP of Sales\", \"draft outreach for this prospect\", \"my cold emails get no replies\".   keywords: "cold email writer, ai cold email generator, b2b cold email template, claude cold email skill, write cold email that gets replies"

  outputs: "Three email variants, Subject lines, Why each angle works"

Use this for the first email to someone who has never heard of you. It produces three short variants, each built on a different angle, so the sender can choose or test.

## Inputs

- Who: the prospect or segment, their role and company.
- Why now: a trigger or research hook, if any.
- What: the offer in one outcome sentence, plus approved proof (a customer, a number, a before and after).

## The play

### 1. Pick one problem
The email is about one problem the reader probably has. Not three benefits, not the product tour. If you cannot name the problem in the reader's words, go back to research.

### 2. Use the four-part frame
1. **Observation** (why them, why now): the trigger or a sharp role insight. One sentence.
2. **Problem**: what that situation usually causes. One or two sentences.
3. **Proof**: a peer who solved it, with a concrete result. One sentence.
4. **Ask**: low-friction, interest-based. "Worth a look?" beats "Do you have 30 minutes Tuesday at 2pm?"

Read [references/cold-email-frameworks.md](references/cold-email-frameworks.md) for alternative frames, annotated examples and the line-by-line edit checklist.

### 3. Write three angles
Typical set: a trigger angle, a pain angle and a peer-proof angle. Each variant is a real alternative, not the same email with synonyms.

### 4. Edit hard
- Under 100 words; 50-80 is the sweet spot.
- Reading level of a smart 12-year-old: short words, short sentences.
- "You" and "your" outnumber "we" and "our".
- No attachments, no images, at most one link (better: none in the first email).
- Read it on a phone. If it needs scrolling, cut.

### 5. Subject lines
Two to four words, lowercase, looks like an internal email: "ramp time", "new sdr team", "question about payroll". Give three per variant.

## Output format

```
Variant A - <angle>
Subject options: <3>
<email>
Why it works: <one line>
```

Repeat for B and C, then a note on which to send first and why.

## What good looks like

- The first line could only be sent to this person or segment.
- The reader understands what you do without a feature list.
- The ask can be answered with one word.
- The proof is specific and approved: a named customer or a precise number, never "leading companies".
- The common mistake is starting with yourself ("I'm X from Y and we...") and ending with a 30-minute meeting request from a stranger.

## Rules

- MUST keep the email under 100 words.
- MUST use only approved proof points.
- NEVER fake familiarity ("Hope you're well", "As we discussed", "Re:" on a first email).
- NEVER invent personalization; use a role-level opener when research found nothing.
- NEVER use spam-trigger formatting: all caps, multiple exclamation marks, "free", "guarantee".

## Example prompts

- "Write a cold email to Dana Kim, Head of SDR at Lumen. They're hiring 4 SDRs. We sell AI list building."
- "Write a segment template for VPs of Operations at 3PLs, with one personalization slot."
- "Our emails get 0.5% replies. Rewrite this one."

references.title: Cold email frameworks
references.markdown:
# Cold email frameworks

## Four frames that work

| Frame | Structure | Best when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Observation → Problem → Proof → Ask | Default | You have a trigger or sharp research |
| Problem → Agitate → Solve (short) | Name the pain, show its cost, hint at the fix | Pain is common and costly for the role |
| Before → After → Bridge | Their likely current state, a peer's better state, how | You have a strong customer story |
| Question-led | A single relevant question, then one line of context | Very senior readers, founders |

## Annotated example

> Subject: new sdr team
>
> Hi Dana, Lumen has four SDR roles open, and the listing says outbound is being built from scratch. ← observation, sourced
>
> New teams usually lose their first month to list building: reps researching accounts instead of talking to them. ← problem, in the reader's world
>
> Northwind had the same setup last spring; their reps booked first meetings in week two instead of week six. ← proof, specific
>
> Worth a look before your new hires start? ← low-friction ask

72 words. One problem. One proof. One-word answer possible.

## Weak to strong rewrites

**Weak opener**: "I hope this email finds you well. My name is Sam and I'm with Acme, the leading AI platform for..."
**Strong**: "Saw the Series B post: doubling the sales team by Q4."

**Weak problem**: "Many companies struggle with efficiency and productivity in their sales processes."
**Strong**: "New reps spend their first month building lists instead of selling."

**Weak proof**: "We work with leading companies across many industries."
**Strong**: "Contoso cut ramp from 5 months to 3."

**Weak ask**: "Do you have 30 minutes this week for a demo?"
**Strong**: "Worth a look?" / "Is that on your radar?" / "Want me to send the two-minute version?"

## Line-by-line edit checklist

1. Delete the first sentence. Is the email better? Then keep it deleted.
2. Every sentence earns its place or goes.
3. Replace adjectives with numbers or names.
4. Swap "we help companies" for what the reader gets.
5. One question mark in the whole email.
6. No links, no attachments in email one.
7. Read aloud; anything you would not say to a peer gets rewritten.

## Personalization slots for segment templates

Keep the template 80% fixed and leave one slot of 1-2 sentences for the personal line. A slot that says `{trigger_sentence}` with a fallback line for when research finds nothing scales better than templates with five merge fields.

Use this for "<competitor> vs <you>", "<competitor> alternatives" and "best <category> for <use case>" pages. Readers on these pages are close to buying; honesty converts them better than spin.

## Inputs

- Competitor research (current pricing with the date checked, features, positioning, reviews).
- Your product facts, pricing and limits.
- Proof: customers who switched, migration stories, review quotes you may use.

## The play

### 1. Pick the page type
| Query | Page | Promise |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "x vs y" | Head-to-head | Help me choose between these two |
| "x alternatives" | List of options, you included | Help me find something better than x |
| "best <category> for <use case>" | Ranked list | Help me shortlist |

### 2. Lead with the verdict
A short answer at the top: who should choose the competitor, who should choose you. Readers and answer engines both pull from it.

### 3. Build the criteria table
Criteria the buyer cares about (not just your strengths): price and pricing model, setup time, key capabilities, limits, integrations, support, best for. Mark facts with a "last checked" date.

### 4. Write the sections
1. Quick verdict.
2. At-a-glance table.
3. Key differences, each with what it means for the buyer.
4. Pricing compared, with a worked example for a typical team.
5. When the competitor is the better choice (yes, really).
6. Switching: effort, what moves over, help offered.
7. FAQ (5-8 questions).
8. CTA that fits: try free, see a migration plan, book a comparison demo.

### 5. Add SEO and schema
Title under 60 characters ("X vs Y: honest comparison for <audience>"), meta under 155, FAQPage schema, internal links to the other comparison pages and the product pages.

## What good looks like

- A reader who should choose the competitor would agree with the page.
- Every factual claim about the competitor is current and checkable.
- The pricing example uses a realistic team, not a cherry-picked one.
- The common mistake is a page where you win every row, which readers distrust and reviewers call out.

## Rules

- MUST date pricing and feature facts about competitors.
- MUST include a "when they are the better choice" section.
- NEVER misstate a competitor's features, prices or limits.
- NEVER use a competitor's logo or trademarks in ways that imply endorsement.

## Example prompts

- "Write a 'Rotaflow vs us' page for multi-location dental groups."
- "Write a 'Top 7 Rotaflow alternatives' page that includes us honestly."
- "Refresh our comparison page pricing table and FAQ."

  category: positioning
  tags: "Sales, Sales Leaders, Marketing, SDR"
  author: prosyo
  version: "1.0.0"
  keywords: "competitive battlecard template, sales battle card, how to beat competitor, claude battlecard skill, competitor talk track"
  inputs: "Competitor research or teardown, Win-loss notes, Your differentiators and proof"
  outputs: "One-page battlecard, Objection responses, Landmine questions"

Use this when a competitor comes up often on calls. A battlecard is the on-call version of a teardown: short enough to read in 30 seconds with the buyer still talking.

## Inputs

- Competitor research (or run a teardown first).
- Win-loss notes against this competitor.
- Your differentiators and approved proof.

## The play

### 1. Lead with when you win and lose
The most useful line on the card. Reps need to know whether to fight or qualify out.

### 2. Write the quick positioning
Two sentences a rep can say when the buyer mentions the competitor, acknowledging their strength and stating your difference fairly.

### 3. Three differentiators with proof
Only differences that matter to buyers and that you can prove. Each: what, why it matters to the buyer, proof.

### 4. Landmine questions
Questions the rep asks that lead the buyer to discover the competitor's weakness on their own. Fair, neutral, answerable.

### 5. Objection responses
"They're cheaper", "They have feature X", "We already use them for Y". One or two lines each.

### 6. Traps
What the competitor says about you and how to answer it; what not to do (trash talk, matching their discount without a trade).

Read [references/battlecard-template.md](references/battlecard-template.md) for the full one-page template and a filled example.

## What good looks like

- Fits on one screen; a rep can find an answer mid-call.
- Fair about the competitor's strengths; buyers trust reps who are.
- Updated each quarter with fresh win-loss notes and pricing.
- The common mistake is a ten-page feature comparison that reps never open on a call.

## Rules

- MUST keep claims about the competitor factual, current and sourced.
- MUST include when to walk away.
- NEVER disparage the competitor or its people.
- NEVER use confidential competitor information.

## Example prompts

- "Make a battlecard against Acme for our mid-market reps."
- "Turn this teardown into a one-page battlecard."
- "What should I say when a prospect says 'Acme is half the price'?"

references.title: Battlecard template
references.markdown:
# Battlecard template

```
COMPETITOR: <name>                              Updated: <month year>

WE WIN WHEN: <2-3 situations>
WE LOSE WHEN: <2-3 situations>  →  Qualify out early by asking: <question>

QUICK POSITIONING (say this):
"<Competitor> is a good fit for <who>. Teams that need <what> usually choose us because <why>."

DIFFERENTIATORS
1. <What> - why it matters - proof
2. <What> - why it matters - proof
3. <What> - why it matters - proof

LANDMINE QUESTIONS
- <question>
- <question>
- <question>

OBJECTIONS
"<objection>" → <response>
"<objection>" → <response>
"<objection>" → <response>

PRICING NOTES: <their model, typical price, renewal behaviour, what is gated>

THEY SAY ABOUT US → WE SAY
"<claim>" → <response>

DON'T: <traps>
```

## Filled example (fictional competitor "Rotaflow")

```
WE WIN WHEN: multi-location groups (10+ sites); teams that need group-level reporting; ops leaders own the decision
WE LOSE WHEN: single-site practices; buyers want the cheapest option; IT mandates their existing suite
  → Qualify out early: "How many locations will be on it in 12 months?"

QUICK POSITIONING:
"Rotaflow is great for single offices that want something simple. Groups with 10+ locations usually pick us because they can move patients and staff across sites from one schedule."

DIFFERENTIATORS
1. Group-level schedule - fill chairs across sites - Northwind: 71% → 86% utilisation
2. Same-day reporting - decisions on today's data - live demo of the group view
3. Rollout in 3 weeks - no lost booking days - rollout plan + 2 references

LANDMINE QUESTIONS
- "How do you see open capacity across all locations today?"
- "What happens when one office is overbooked and the next one is empty?"
- "How long did rollout take for groups your size?"

OBJECTIONS
"Rotaflow is cheaper per location." → "It is. Most groups find one extra filled chair a day per site covers the difference; want to run your numbers?"
"We already use Rotaflow at two sites." → "Makes sense to start there. How do you combine their schedules with the other eight?"

DON'T: call them outdated; promise features on the roadmap; match their price without a trade
```

Use this when a competitor shows up in deals often enough to matter. It produces a teardown that tells sales where to fight, where to walk away and what to say.

## Inputs

- Competitor name and site.
- Your own positioning, product scope and pricing.
- Win-loss notes or rep anecdotes involving this competitor. Even five are useful.

## The play

### 1. Read their story
Homepage headline, category they claim, the customer logos they lead with, the use cases on their navigation. Write their positioning in one sentence as they would: "For <who>, <product> is the <category> that <benefit>."

### 2. Map pricing and packaging
Plans, price points, what is gated to higher tiers, contract terms, free trial or not. Packaging choices reveal who they want and who they tolerate.

### 3. Mine customer complaints
Read reviews (lowest ratings first), community threads and public support forums. Cluster complaints into themes and count them. Recurring themes with 5+ mentions are real weaknesses; single rants are not.

### 4. Map their sales motion
Self-serve or sales-led, demo gating, typical discount behaviour, implementation time, who they target in the buying committee.

### 5. Read recent moves
Launches, pricing changes, leadership hires, funding, layoffs from the last 12 months. Direction of travel matters more than today's feature list.

### 6. Decide where to compete
Use the matrix in [references/teardown-template.md](references/teardown-template.md): segments where you win, where you tie and where you lose. Losing segments are as valuable as winning ones; they tell reps when to qualify out early.

## Output format

```
Competitor: <name>  |  Their positioning: <one sentence>
Who they win: <segments>         Who they struggle with: <segments>
Pricing: <summary>               Packaging traps: <what is gated>
Strengths (be honest): <3>
Weaknesses (evidence): <3, with count of mentions and source>
Recent moves: <dated>
Where we compete: <segments + win theme>
Where we avoid: <segments + early qualify-out question>
Talk track: <3 lines a rep can say, no trash talk>
Landmines: <questions that expose their weak spots, asked neutrally>
```

## What good looks like

- Honest strengths. A teardown that says the competitor is bad at everything gets ignored by reps who just lost to them.
- Weaknesses come with evidence and counts.
- Landmine questions are neutral and fair: "How long did implementation take for teams your size?" not "Did you know they're terrible at onboarding?"
- It answers when to walk away. The best teams lose fewer deals by qualifying out of the wrong ones faster.

## Rules

- MUST use public sources or your own deal notes, and cite them.
- MUST date pricing; pricing pages change often.
- NEVER disparage the competitor in rep-facing copy.
- NEVER use confidential material obtained from a competitor's employees or customers under NDA.

## Example prompts

- "Do a teardown of Northbeam versus us. We lose to them in mid-market."
- "A new competitor just launched. Tear them down from their site and reviews."
- "Turn these 14 loss notes against Acme into a teardown and talk track."
