references.title: Filter recipes
references.markdown:
# Filter recipes

## Title keyword patterns

Titles are messy. Use include and exclude keyword sets rather than exact titles.

| Persona | Include | Exclude |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sales leader | VP Sales, Head of Sales, Chief Revenue, CRO, Sales Director | Assistant, Intern, Coordinator, "Sales Operations" (separate persona) |
| SDR leader | Sales Development, SDR Manager, BDR Manager, Head of SDR | Representative, Associate |
| RevOps | Revenue Operations, Sales Operations, RevOps, GTM Operations | Analyst (unless targeting users) |
| Marketing leader | CMO, VP Marketing, Head of Marketing, Head of Growth, Demand Generation | Coordinator, Specialist, Intern |
| Operations | COO, VP Operations, Head of Operations, Director of Operations | Operations Assistant, Clerk |
| Founder | Founder, Co-founder, CEO (at under 50 employees) | Founder of unrelated side businesses (check the company) |

Seniority filters alone miss titles like "Head of"; keyword includes catch them.

## Exclusions people forget

- **Lookalike vendors.** Searching "payroll" returns payroll software companies, not companies with payroll pain.
- **Agencies and consultants** who describe themselves with your buyer's keywords.
- **Subsidiaries and parents** of current customers.
- **Former customers** who churned in the last 6 months (route to a win-back play instead).
- **Recruiters and job seekers** whose headlines contain the target title.
- **Students and "aspiring" profiles.**
- **Investors** at firms with your target industry in their description.

## Size bands that behave differently

| Headcount | Typical buyer | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1-10 | Founder | Fast, price-sensitive, decides alone |
| 11-50 | Founder or first functional leader | Buyer is often also the user |
| 51-200 | Functional leader (VP, Head of) | First process and tool decisions |
| 201-1,000 | Director plus VP sign-off | Committee forms, procurement appears |
| 1,000+ | Committee | Security review, long cycles, multi-threading required |

## Recipe example

```
Accounts: industry = logistics, 3PL, freight forwarding
          headcount 50-500
          region = US, Canada
          hiring: any open role containing "operations" or "warehouse" in last 60 days
          exclude: description contains "software", "platform", "SaaS"
Contacts: include VP Operations, Director of Operations, Head of Operations, COO
          exclude assistant, coordinator, intern
          max 2 per account
Expected: about 1,100 accounts, about 1,700 contacts before cleaning
```

Use this when you need a reason for buyers to raise their hand. The best lead magnets solve one small, urgent part of the buyer's problem and lead naturally to the bigger part your product solves.

## Inputs

- Persona, their problem and the job they are trying to do.
- The product and where it fits in that job.
- Where the magnet will be promoted (LinkedIn, ads, SEO, outbound).

## The play

### 1. Pick the format by intent
| Format | Works when | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Template | The buyer has to produce something | "Mutual action plan template" |
| Checklist | The buyer fears missing something | "Cold email deliverability checklist" |
| Calculator or free tool | The buyer needs a number or a quick result | "Sending capacity calculator" |
| Benchmark report | The buyer wants to compare themselves | "Outbound reply rates by industry" |
| Swipe file | The buyer wants examples to copy | "50 cold emails that got replies" |
| Mini course | The buyer needs a skill, over days | "5-day LinkedIn outreach course" |

### 2. Pass the bridge test
Using the magnet should make the buyer more likely to need your product. A deliverability checklist for a sending tool passes; a generic productivity ebook does not.

### 3. Draft it
Specific and usable in under 30 minutes. One problem, solved well. Include real examples and numbers.

### 4. Write the landing page
Headline with the outcome, three bullets of what is inside, a preview image or sample, a short form (email, and maybe company), and a thank-you page with a useful next step.

### 5. Write the follow-up
Three to five emails: deliver the asset, a tip for using it, a related story, then a soft invitation to the product. Route leads by fit: ICP leads with high-intent actions go to sales; the rest stay in nurture.

### 6. Decide gating
Gate when the asset is substantial and the audience is qualified; leave ungated (and capture with a softer ask) when reach and SEO matter more. Many teams gate the editable version and publish the preview openly.

## What good looks like

- Downloaders are mostly ICP buyers.
- The magnet is used, not just downloaded: templates get filled in, calculators get run.
- The follow-up gets replies, not only unsubscribes.
- The common mistake is a 40-page ebook nobody finishes, gated behind a 9-field form.

## Rules

- MUST make the asset genuinely useful on its own.
- MUST tell people what they will receive and how often they will hear from you, and honour unsubscribes.
- NEVER pass downloaders to sales as "hot leads" without fit and intent.
- NEVER use other companies' data or content without permission.

## Example prompts

- "Give me 10 lead magnet ideas for selling to heads of RevOps, ranked."
- "Build a 'cold email deliverability checklist' lead magnet with landing page and follow-ups."
- "Turn our benchmark data into a gated report."

Use this when the question is "which leads should sales call first?". It produces a scoring model with point tables, a threshold and a validation test, documented well enough that anyone can configure it.

## Inputs

- 6 to 12 months of leads with outcome: became an opportunity, won, or went nowhere.
- Firmographic and role data on each lead.
- Engagement events: form fills, page visits, email replies, event attendance, product sign-ups.
- Sales capacity: how many leads a week the team can work properly.

## The play

### 1. Two axes, never one
- **Fit** (who they are): role, company size, industry, region, stack. Changes rarely.
- **Engagement** (what they did): actions, weighted by intent, decaying over time.

A single blended number lets a student who downloads ten ebooks outrank a VP who visited pricing once.

### 2. Derive points from data
For each attribute and action, compare the opportunity rate of leads that have it with the base rate. Points roughly follow the lift: an action with 4x the base opportunity rate earns about twice the points of one with 2x. Read [references/scoring-tables.md](references/scoring-tables.md) for starter tables and the lift method.

### 3. Add negative scores and decay
Subtract for students, competitors, personal emails, job seekers and unsubscribes. Halve engagement points every 30 days so old activity does not keep a lead hot.

### 4. Set the threshold from capacity
Choose the fit and engagement cut-offs that send sales roughly the number of leads they can work within the SLA. A threshold that produces 300 leads a week for a team that can work 80 trains reps to ignore scores.

### 5. Define the handoff
- High fit + high engagement: route to sales, first touch within 1 business hour (inbound) or same day.
- High fit + low engagement: targeted outbound or nurture.
- Low fit + high engagement: self-serve path or marketing nurture.
- Low fit + low engagement: no action.

High-intent actions such as a demo request or pricing contact bypass scoring entirely.

### 6. Validate before launch
Backtest on last quarter: the top 20% of scored leads should hold at least 50% of the opportunities. Then review monthly.

## What good looks like

- Sales can explain any score from the point table in 30 seconds.
- The top-scored decile converts to opportunity at 3x or more the average.
- Demo requests never wait for a score.
- The common mistake is guessing points in a meeting ("a webinar feels like 10 points") instead of deriving them from outcomes.

## Rules

- MUST keep fit and engagement as separate scores.
- MUST include decay and negative scoring.
- MUST backtest before going live.
- NEVER route a direct demo or pricing request through scoring delays.

## Example prompts

- "Build a lead scoring model from this export of 4,000 leads with outcomes."
- "Our MQLs convert at 3%. Redesign the scoring so sales trusts it."
- "Set a threshold that sends my 5 reps about 60 leads a week."

references.title: Scoring tables
references.markdown:
# Scoring tables

## Lift method

1. Base rate: share of all leads that became an opportunity. Example: 4%.
2. For each attribute or action, its opportunity rate. Example: leads who visited pricing, 14%.
3. Lift = rate ÷ base. Pricing visit lift = 3.5.
4. Points ≈ 10 × log2(lift), rounded. Lift 2 → 10 points, lift 4 → 20, lift 8 → 30. Lift below 1.2 → 0. Lift below 0.8 → negative.

Only trust lifts computed on 30+ leads with that attribute.

## Starter fit table (replace with your lifts)

| Attribute | Points |
| --- | --- |
| Title in buyer persona | +25 |
| Title in champion persona | +20 |
| Company size in sweet spot | +20 |
| Target industry | +15 |
| Target region | +10 |
| Uses an integrated technology | +10 |
| Personal email domain | -20 |
| Student, intern, job seeker | -50 |
| Competitor domain | -100 |

## Starter engagement table

| Action | Points | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pricing page visit | +20 | Count once per 7 days |
| Comparison or alternatives page visit | +15 | |
| Case study view | +10 | |
| Product sign-up or trial start | +30 | |
| Replied to an email | +25 | Any reply, triaged separately |
| Webinar attended live | +15 | Registered only: +5 |
| Content download | +5 | Diminishing: cap at +15 total |
| Email opened | 0 | Unreliable signal; ignore |
| Unsubscribed | -30 | |
| Demo request | Route directly | Bypasses scoring |

Decay: engagement points halve every 30 days.

## Thresholds

Start with fit ≥ 60 and engagement ≥ 40 for sales handoff, then tune weekly in the first month until the volume matches capacity.

## Monthly review table

| Score band | Leads | Opportunities | Rate | Lift vs base |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Top 10% | | | | target 3x+ |
| 10-30% | | | | |
| 30-100% | | | | |

Use this to warm up Tier 1 buyers before outreach. A few thoughtful comments on a buyer's posts over two weeks make your later connection request familiar rather than cold.

## Inputs

- Target buyers (and whether they post), plus the industry voices they engage with.
- Topics the commenter can speak to with real experience.
- Time available: 15-30 minutes a day is enough.

## The play

### 1. Build the watch list
- **Buyers who post**: comment on their posts directly.
- **Buyers who don't post**: find the voices and communities they engage with; comment there, where they read.
- 20-40 people on the list at a time.

### 2. Write comments that add something
| Comment type | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Add an insight | "We saw the same thing; the twist for us was that approvals, not accounting, drove the delay." |
| Add a number or example | "One team I work with went from 9 days to 4 by adding a day-3 cut-off." |
| Ask a sharp question | "Did the 6-day close hold through quarter end, or does that need a different playbook?" |
| Respectful disagreement | "Agree on the goal, but in our experience the tool came last, not first." |

Two to four sentences. No pitch, no links, no "Great post!".

### 3. Keep a rhythm
Per day: 5-10 comments, mostly on target buyers' content and the voices they follow. Reply to replies on your comments within a few hours; those threads are where real conversations start.

### 4. Convert to connection
After two or three meaningful interactions, send a connection request that references the thread. Then the first message continues the topic.

## What good looks like

- The buyer replies to your comment, or likes it, before you ever send a request.
- Comments would be useful to any reader of the post, not only the author.
- The common mistake is "Great insights, thanks for sharing!" on 50 posts a day, which builds nothing and looks automated.

## Rules

- MUST add a genuine insight, example or question in each comment.
- MUST draw only on the commenter's real experience.
- NEVER pitch or link to your product in a comment on someone else's post.
- NEVER automate comments.

## Example prompts

- "Set up a 2-week comment plan to warm up these 15 CFOs before outreach."
- "Write a thoughtful comment on this post from a VP Sales about SDR ramp."
- "Which voices do heads of RevOps follow, so I can show up there?"

Use this for the first step of LinkedIn outreach. The note has one job: get accepted by giving a genuine reason to connect. Selling comes later, and only if the conversation earns it.

## Inputs

- The prospect: name, role, company, recent activity.
- The reason to connect: shared topic, trigger, event, community, mutual connection, their content.
- Who you are, in a few words.

## The play

### 1. Find the reason
| Reason | Strength | Note pattern |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Referral from a mutual connection | Strongest | "Sam suggested we connect about..." (only if true) |
| They engaged with your content | Strong | "Thanks for your comment on..." |
| Same event or community | Strong | "Saw you're at <event> next week too..." |
| Their content | Strong | "Your post on <specific point>..." |
| Role or industry peer | Medium | "I work with a lot of <role>s in <industry>..." |
| Trigger (new role, hiring) | Medium | "Congrats on <role>, <specific note>" |

### 2. Write the note
- Under 200 characters; shorter is usually better. Free accounts may have a lower limit and a monthly cap on notes, so check yours.
- One reason, one sentence about it, no ask beyond the connection.
- No links, no product, no "I'd love to tell you about".

### 3. Decide whether to send a note at all
For senior executives with no real hook, and for people who post a lot and connect openly, a blank request often performs as well or better. Test both on 100+ requests before deciding.

### 4. Plan the first message after acceptance
Write it now, so acceptance leads into a conversation within 1-3 days while you are still recognised.

## Examples

- Content: "Your post on why SDR ramp is a data problem made me rethink our onboarding. Would be good to connect."
- Event: "See you're at the RevOps summit next week, I'll be there too. Happy to connect beforehand."
- Peer: "I spend most of my week with heads of ops at multi-site restaurant groups. Would be good to have you in my network."
- New role: "Congrats on the move to Fabrikam. Building ops from scratch at that stage is a fun problem."

## What good looks like

- Acceptance rate of 30-50% on a targeted list. Under 20% means the targeting or the note is wrong.
- Nothing in the note could be called a pitch.
- The common mistake is the "pitch in the invite": a note that ends in "would love to show you how we help companies like yours".

## Rules

- MUST stay under the character limit of the user's account.
- MUST use a real reason; never invent a mutual connection, event or shared interest.
- NEVER pitch or include links in a connection note.
- NEVER exceed safe daily invitation volumes (typically 15-25 per day per account).

## Example prompts

- "Write connection notes for these 25 VPs of Sales. Most have posted about hiring."
- "My acceptance rate is 12%. Rewrite my note."
- "Write notes for people attending the same conference as me."
skills.html:
Use this for the first step of LinkedIn outreach. The note has one job: get accepted by giving a genuine reason to connect. Selling comes later, and only if the conversation earns it.

Inputs

  • The prospect: name, role, company, recent activity.
  • The reason to connect: shared topic, trigger, event, community, mutual connection, their content.
  • Who you are, in a few words.

The play

1. Find the reason

ReasonStrengthNote pattern
Referral from a mutual connectionStrongest"Sam suggested we connect about..." (only if true)
They engaged with your contentStrong"Thanks for your comment on..."
Same event or communityStrong"Saw you're at <event> next week too..."
Their contentStrong"Your post on <specific point>..."
Role or industry peerMedium"I work with a lot of <role>s in <industry>..."
Trigger (new role, hiring)Medium"Congrats on <role>, <specific note>"

2. Write the note

  • Under 200 characters; shorter is usually better. Free accounts may have a lower limit and a monthly cap on notes, so check yours.
  • One reason, one sentence about it, no ask beyond the connection.
  • No links, no product, no "I'd love to tell you about".

3. Decide whether to send a note at all

For senior executives with no real hook, and for people who post a lot and connect openly, a blank request often performs as well or better. Test both on 100+ requests before deciding.

4. Plan the first message after acceptance

Write it now, so acceptance leads into a conversation within 1-3 days while you are still recognised.

Examples

  • Content: "Your post on why SDR ramp is a data problem made me rethink our onboarding. Would be good to connect."
  • Event: "See you're at the RevOps summit next week, I'll be there too. Happy to connect beforehand."
  • Peer: "I spend most of my week with heads of ops at multi-site restaurant groups. Would be good to have you in my network."
  • New role: "Congrats on the move to Fabrikam. Building ops from scratch at that stage is a fun problem."

What good looks like

  • Acceptance rate of 30-50% on a targeted list. Under 20% means the targeting or the note is wrong.
  • Nothing in the note could be called a pitch.
  • The common mistake is the "pitch in the invite": a note that ends in "would love to show you how we help companies like yours".

Rules

  • MUST stay under the character limit of the user's account.
  • MUST use a real reason; never invent a mutual connection, event or shared interest.
  • NEVER pitch or include links in a connection note.
  • NEVER exceed safe daily invitation volumes (typically 15-25 per day per account).

Example prompts

  • "Write connection notes for these 25 VPs of Sales. Most have posted about hiring."
  • "My acceptance rate is 12%. Rewrite my note."
  • "Write notes for people attending the same conference as me."

Use this to plan a LinkedIn campaign end to end. LinkedIn is a conversation channel; messages that read like emails pasted into a chat window get ignored.

## Inputs

- Persona and the problem the campaign is about.
- Offer and approved proof.
- The reason to connect (from research, an event, content or a trigger).

## The play

### 1. Shape the sequence
| Step | Timing | Job | Length |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Connection request | Day 0 | Get accepted | Under 200 characters, no pitch |
| Message 1 | 1-3 days after accept | Start a conversation on the topic | 1-3 sentences, ends in a question |
| Message 2 | 4-5 days later | Give value: an insight, resource or story | 2-4 sentences |
| Message 3 | 5-7 days later | Soft ask tied to their answer or the topic | 2-3 sentences |
| Message 4 | 7-10 days later | Close the loop warmly | 1-2 sentences |

Voice notes and short videos can replace message 2 or 3 for Tier 1 contacts; they stand out because few people use them.

### 2. Write like a chat
Short lines, no subject, no sign-off block, no bullet lists, no links in message 1. Ask questions people can answer from their phone in five seconds.

### 3. Bridge from topic to problem
Message 1 is about the topic that made you connect. The bridge to your problem comes through their answer, or in message 2 with a peer insight. Read [references/linkedin-sequence-example.md](references/linkedin-sequence-example.md) for a full example with reply branches.

### 4. Handle replies fast
LinkedIn replies expect a response within hours. Positive replies get a meeting link or two time options; questions get a direct answer, not a pitch.

### 5. Exit rules
Stop on any reply (switch to manual), if they decline, or if someone at the same account books a meeting. Withdraw connection requests not accepted after 14-21 days.

## What good looks like

- Message 1 gets a reply because it is a question about their world, not your product.
- No message is longer than a phone screen.
- Acceptance 30%+, reply rate on accepted connections 15-25%+ for a well-targeted list.
- The common mistake is "Thanks for connecting! We help companies like yours..." sent seconds after acceptance.

## Rules

- MUST wait at least a day after acceptance before the first message.
- MUST stop automation the moment someone replies.
- MUST stay within safe daily limits for invitations and messages.
- NEVER pitch in the connection note or message 1.
- NEVER send links in the first message.

## Example prompts

- "Build a LinkedIn sequence for heads of finance at 50-200 person companies. Problem: slow month-end close."
- "What should I send after people accept my connection request?"
- "Rewrite our LinkedIn messages; they read like emails."

references.title: LinkedIn sequence example with reply branches
references.markdown:
# LinkedIn sequence example with reply branches

Persona: Heads of Finance at 50-200 person companies. Topic: month-end close.

**Connection note**
> Your post on cutting close from 10 days to 6 had some smart ideas. Would be good to connect.

**Message 1 (2 days after accept)**
> Thanks for connecting, Maya. Curious: of the ideas in your post, which one actually saved the most time? The approval cut-off one surprised me.

**Message 2 (5 days later, if no reply)**
> One thing I keep hearing from finance leads at your size: the accounting is fast, it's the last-week approvals that drag. A controller at Contoso fixed it with a day-3 cut-off and one approval queue, and got to a 4-day close. Does that match what you see?

**Message 3 (6 days later)**
> If it's useful, I can send the checklist Contoso used. It's a one-pager, no strings. Want it?

**Message 4 (8 days later)**
> Will leave it here, Maya. If close time becomes a priority again, happy to compare notes anytime.

## Reply branches

| Their reply | Your answer |
| --- | --- |
| Answers the question (engaged) | Respond to what they said first; then share one relevant insight; ask if the problem is live for them now |
| "Sure, send it" | Send the asset, then: "Happy to walk you through how they rolled it out, 15 minutes this week or next?" |
| "What do you do?" | One sentence of what you do and for whom, one proof point, then a question about their situation |
| "Not a priority" | "Makes sense, thanks for saying so. Mind if I check back in a quarter?" |
| "We already use a tool for that" | "Got it. Out of curiosity, how long does close take with it today?" (only if genuinely curious; otherwise thank them) |
| "Not interested" / "Stop" | "Understood, I won't message again." Then stop everywhere. |

## Timing guardrails

- Send during their working hours, weekdays.
- No more than one unanswered message every 4 days.
- Total LinkedIn messages without a reply: 4 at most.

Use this to turn an idea, a customer story or an opinion into a post the right buyers read and respond to. Posts that build pipeline teach buyers something about their own problem; posts that only build reach entertain peers.

## Inputs

- The idea, story, lesson or data point.
- Two or three past posts or messages by the author, for voice.
- The target buyer and the problem space.

## The play

### 1. Pick a format
| Format | Shape | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Story | Situation → tension → turn → lesson | Founders, customer moments |
| Lesson list | Hook → 3-7 numbered lessons → takeaway | Experience-based expertise |
| Contrarian take | Common belief → why it's wrong → what works | Standing out in a crowded topic |
| How-to | Problem → steps → result | Practical, saveable content |
| Data post | Surprising number → what it means → what to do | Credibility with analytical buyers |
| Behind the scenes | What we tried → what happened → what we learned | Trust, transparency |

Read [references/post-formats.md](references/post-formats.md) for a template and an example of each.

### 2. Write the hook
The first two lines decide whether anyone clicks "see more". Hooks that work: a specific number, a counter-intuitive claim, a vivid moment, or the reader's exact problem. Avoid questions as the very first line and avoid "I'm excited to announce".

### 3. Make the body skimmable
One idea per line or short paragraph. White space. No more than 1,300 characters for most posts; long only when the story earns it. No external links in the post body; put them in a comment if needed.

### 4. End with a conversation
A specific question invites comments from buyers: "How long does month-end take your team?" beats "Thoughts?".

### 5. Match the voice
Use the author's words, sentence length and level of formality. A founder who writes plainly should not suddenly sound like a motivational speaker.

## What good looks like

- A buyer would save it or send it to a colleague.
- The hook is specific; the lesson is earned by the story.
- The common mistake is broetry: one-line dramatic sentences, a fake story, and a lesson nobody needed. Readers spot it and so does the algorithm's audience.

## Rules

- MUST keep stories and numbers true; ask the author for details rather than invent them.
- MUST match the author's voice and approve before posting.
- NEVER name customers or share their results without approval.
- NEVER engagement-bait ("comment YES to get the guide") unless the user explicitly chooses that tactic.

## Example prompts

- "Turn this customer story into a LinkedIn post for our founder."
- "Write a contrarian post about why more SDRs doesn't mean more pipeline."
- "Plan 8 posts for the next month aimed at heads of RevOps."

# Post formats with examples

## Story

```
Hook: the moment, specific and vivid
Tension: what was at stake
Turn: what changed
Lesson: one sentence the reader can use
Question: invite their version
```

> Our best customer almost churned in month two.
>
> Their ops lead, Priya, emailed: "We're spending more time on this than on the old spreadsheet."
>
> We had built a beautiful onboarding. She needed one thing: her existing shift codes imported.
>
> We did it by hand that afternoon. She renewed for three years.
>
> Lesson: the fastest onboarding is the one that starts from the customer's mess, not your template.
>
> What's the one thing that made you stick with a tool?

## Lesson list

> I've reviewed 400 cold emails this year. The ones that got replies had five things in common:
>
> 1. Under 90 words
> 2. One problem, not three
> 3. A named peer, not "leading companies"
> 4. No links in the first email
> 5. An ask you can answer with one word
>
> The ones that failed usually started with "I hope this finds you well".
>
> Which of these do you break most often?

## Contrarian take

> Hiring more SDRs won't fix your pipeline.
>
> Most teams that double SDR headcount see meetings per rep drop by a third. Same list, more people fishing in it.
>
> The fix is upstream: better accounts, better timing, better first lines.
>
> Before you open four reqs, check how many accounts in your ICP haven't been touched this quarter.
>
> Agree or disagree?

## How-to

Hook with the result, then numbered steps, then the outcome and a question.

## Data post

> 62% of the "no replies" in our last campaign were never delivered to the inbox.
>
> The copy wasn't the problem. The domain was.
>
> Here's the 10-minute check we now run before every campaign: ...

## Behind the scenes

What we tried, the numbers, what surprised us, what we'd do differently. Honest numbers, including the bad ones, build the most trust.

| --- | --- | --- |
| Tue | Lesson list or how-to | A practical fix |
| Thu | Story or contrarian take | A belief to challenge |
| Optional | Data or behind the scenes | Proof and credibility |

Use this before running LinkedIn outreach. Prospects look at your profile before accepting or replying; a resume-style profile tells them you want something from them, a buyer-focused one tells them why talking to you is useful.

## Inputs

- The current profile text: headline, About, experience, featured.
- Who you sell to and the problem you solve.
- Proof: results, customers you can name, content you have made.

## The play

### 1. Headline: who you help and with what
Formula: **I help <who> <achieve outcome or fix problem>** | proof or specialism. Under 220 characters, front-loaded because only the first part shows in search and invitations.

- Resume: "Account Executive at Acme"
- Buyer-focused: "Helping restaurant groups close payroll in a day, not a week | Account Executive at Acme"

### 2. About section: the buyer's story
Read [references/profile-templates.md](references/profile-templates.md) for the About structure and three examples. Short version:
1. A first line about the reader's problem (only the first lines show before "see more").
2. What you have seen working with people like them.
3. How you help, in plain words.
4. Proof: one or two results.
5. A low-pressure invitation to talk.

### 3. Featured and banner
- Banner: one line on what you help with, plus a visual cue of the product or result. Not a stock skyline.
- Featured: a customer story, a useful resource and your best post. No product brochure as the first item.

### 4. Experience
Current role written for buyers: what customers get from working with you, not your quota attainment. Earlier roles: one line each unless they add credibility with this buyer.

### 5. The prospect test
Read the top of the profile as a target buyer, on a phone, for five seconds. Do they know who you help and why it matters to them?

## What good looks like

- The headline names the buyer and the outcome.
- The first two lines of About are about the reader.
- Proof is specific and true.
- The common mistake is "President's Club 3x, 147% of quota", which impresses your manager and signals to buyers that they are a target.

## Rules

- MUST keep every claim true and approved for public use.
- MUST write the first lines of the headline and About for the buyer.
- NEVER invent clients, results or titles.

## Example prompts

- "Rewrite my LinkedIn profile. I'm an SDR selling cybersecurity to mid-market IT leaders."
- "Give me 5 headline options for a founder selling to restaurant groups."
- "Review my profile as if you were a VP Sales I'm prospecting."

  1. A first line about the reader's problem (only the first lines show before "see more").
  2. What you have seen working with people like them.
  3. How you help, in plain words.
  4. Proof: one or two results.
  5. A low-pressure invitation to talk.

3. Featured and banner

  • Banner: one line on what you help with, plus a visual cue of the product or result. Not a stock skyline.
  • Featured: a customer story, a useful resource and your best post. No product brochure as the first item.

4. Experience

Current role written for buyers: what customers get from working with you, not your quota attainment. Earlier roles: one line each unless they add credibility with this buyer.

5. The prospect test

Read the top of the profile as a target buyer, on a phone, for five seconds. Do they know who you help and why it matters to them?

What good looks like

  • The headline names the buyer and the outcome.
  • The first two lines of About are about the reader.
  • Proof is specific and true.
  • The common mistake is "President's Club 3x, 147% of quota", which impresses your manager and signals to buyers that they are a target.

Rules

  • MUST keep every claim true and approved for public use.
  • MUST write the first lines of the headline and About for the buyer.
  • NEVER invent clients, results or titles.

Example prompts

  • "Rewrite my LinkedIn profile. I'm an SDR selling cybersecurity to mid-market IT leaders."
  • "Give me 5 headline options for a founder selling to restaurant groups."
  • "Review my profile as if you were a VP Sales I'm prospecting."

references.markdown:
# Profile templates

## About structure

```
Line 1-2: The reader's problem, in their words. (Shows before "see more".)
Para 2:   What you have seen across many teams like theirs (pattern, insight).
Para 3:   How you help, in one or two plain sentences.
Para 4:   Proof: one or two specific results or customers (approved).
Para 5:   Low-pressure invitation + how to reach you.
```

Keep it to 120-250 words. Short paragraphs, no bullet walls.

## Example: SDR, cybersecurity, mid-market IT

> Most IT leaders at 200-1,000 person companies I talk to have the same problem: a security tool stack that grew faster than the team that runs it.
>
> I spend my week with those teams, and the pattern is consistent. Alerts pile up, nobody owns triage, and the audit is always three months away.
>
> At Acme, I help IT leaders find out where their real exposure is in a 30-minute review, before they spend a cent.
>
> Last quarter that review helped a logistics company cut their open critical findings from 140 to 12 ahead of an audit.
>
> If security debt is on your list this year, happy to compare notes. No pitch unless you ask for one.

## Example: Founder, restaurant payroll

> Running payroll for ten restaurants should not take your ops manager three days every two weeks.
>
> I started Acme after watching my family's restaurant group do exactly that: tips, split shifts and three states of tax rules, reconciled by hand.
>
> We built payroll for multi-location restaurant groups: tips, shifts and taxes handled in one run.
>
> Groups like Northwind now close payroll in under a day.
>
> If you run 5+ locations, I'd love to hear how you handle payroll today.

## Example: Agency owner, outbound for B2B SaaS

> Most B2B SaaS teams don't have a lead problem. They have a "the right accounts never hear from us at the right moment" problem.
>
> We run outbound for SaaS companies between $2M and $20M ARR: targeting, copy, sending infrastructure and reply handling.
>
> Clients like Contoso added 40 qualified meetings a quarter without hiring SDRs.
>
> If outbound is on your plan this year, send me a message and I'll share how we would approach your market.

## Headline bank

- Helping <who> <outcome> | <role> at <company>
- <Outcome> for <who> | <proof>
- I help <who> fix <problem> | ex-<credible company>
- <Who>'s go-to for <topic> | <role>

Use this before any list touches a sequence or a CRM import. It produces a clean list and a report of exactly what was removed or changed and why.

## Inputs

- The raw list.
- Suppression sources: customers, open opportunities, opt-outs, do-not-contact, recent contacts.
- The campaign it is for, so you know which columns must be filled.

## The play

### 1. Profile the file
Count rows, columns, blanks per column, and obvious junk (test rows, header repeats, rows with only an email). Note the encoding problems: broken accents in names are common and visible in a first line.

### 2. Normalise
- **Names**: proper case, strip titles and suffixes (Dr., PhD, MBA), split full names, fix all-caps. Keep particles like "van", "de", "Mc" correct.
- **Companies**: strip legal suffixes for display (Inc., Ltd, GmbH, LLC) while keeping the original in another column. "Acme Holdings Inc." becomes "Acme" in an email.
- **Titles**: keep the original, add a normalised seniority and function column.
- **Domains**: lower case, strip www and paths, derive from email when missing.

Read [references/cleaning-rules.md](references/cleaning-rules.md) for the full normalisation and risk rules with edge cases.

### 3. Deduplicate
Match on email first, then on LinkedIn URL, then on first name + last name + domain. Keep the most complete record and merge the rest.

### 4. Remove risk
Drop invalid emails, disposable domains, role addresses (info@, sales@, admin@, support@), personal domains for B2B campaigns, and anything that bounced before. Flag catch-all domains rather than dropping them; decide by campaign size.

### 5. Suppress
Remove customers, open deals, opt-outs and anyone contacted in the last 90 days. Match suppression on email and on domain where the list is account-level.

### 6. Report
Show what happened to every removed row and hand back a list of rows that need a human decision.

## Output format

```
Input: N rows  →  Output: N send-ready rows
Fixed: N names, N company names, N domains
Removed: N duplicates | N invalid | N role | N personal | N disposable | N suppressed (by reason)
Flagged for review: N catch-all | N missing first name | N possible job change
Files: clean list, removed rows with reason, review list
```

## What good looks like

- A random 20-row sample reads perfectly in a merge preview: "Hi Ana," at "Northwind", never "Hi ANA" at "Northwind Holdings, Inc.".
- Removed rows keep their reason, so nothing disappears silently.
- Bounce rate on the cleaned list stays under 2%.
- The common mistake is deduplicating only on email, which leaves the same person in the list twice with a work and an old address.

## Rules

- MUST keep the original values alongside normalised ones.
- MUST output a removed-rows file with reasons.
- NEVER delete records from the user's CRM; cleaning produces new files or proposed changes for approval.
- NEVER guess an email address and mark it as verified.

## Example prompts

- "Clean this 3,500-row CSV for a cold email campaign."
- "Dedupe these two lists and remove our customers."
- "Fix the names and company names so merge fields look natural."

references.title: Cleaning rules
references.markdown:
# Cleaning rules

## Names

| Raw | Clean | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| JOHN SMITH | John Smith | Proper case all-caps names |
| john o'neil | John O'Neil | Capitalise after apostrophe |
| Dr. Sarah Lee, PhD | Sarah Lee | Strip honorifics and post-nominals |
| Ludwig van Beethoven | Ludwig van Beethoven | Keep lowercase particles: van, von, de, da, di, le |
| mcdonald | McDonald | Mc and Mac prefixes (check Mack, Macy exceptions) |
| J. | (flag) | Initial only: not usable as a first name |
| Jos├⌐ | José | Fix encoding before anything else |

## Companies

Strip for display: Inc, Inc., LLC, Ltd, Ltd., Limited, GmbH, AG, SA, S.A., BV, Pty Ltd, PLC, Corp, Corporation, Co., Holdings, Group (only when it is a suffix and the remainder is still recognisable).

Keep: "The" at the start only when it is how the company refers to itself. Brand casing like "eBay" or "iRobot" should be kept exactly as the company writes it on its site.

## Email risk

| Status | Action for cold email |
| --- | --- |
| Valid | Keep |
| Invalid, unknown mailbox | Remove |
| Catch-all (accept-all domain) | Keep for small Tier 1 lists; remove for volume campaigns or send to them last |
| Role address (info@, sales@, hello@, admin@, support@, careers@) | Remove |
| Disposable or temporary domain | Remove |
| Personal domain on a B2B list | Remove, or keep only if the person is a sole founder and the domain is their business |
| Previously bounced | Remove |

## Stale contacts

Flag for review when:
- The last verification is over 90 days old.
- The title or company in the list differs from the current public profile.
- The email domain differs from the company domain (possible acquisition or old job).

## Duplicate merge priority

When merging, keep values from the record with, in order: verified email, most recent update, most filled columns. Never merge two people who share only a first name and a domain.

Use this when your best customers are the clearest definition of your ICP. It produces a ranked list of companies that look like them, each with the reason it matched and the customer story to lead with.

## Inputs

- 5 to 20 best customers, ranked by value and fit.
- Why each one bought, in a line.
- Exclusions: current customers, open deals, competitors, partners.

## The play

### 1. Profile the seeds
For each seed customer, capture the traits that mattered: industry niche (not just industry), business model, headcount band, growth stage, region, technologies, team structure, the trigger that preceded the deal. Look for the 3-5 traits most seeds share; ignore traits only one or two have.

### 2. Weight the traits
Not every shared trait predicts a win. Weight by how specific it is: "sells to restaurants through a field sales team" matters more than "B2B, 50-200 employees".

### 3. Search in widening circles
1. Direct peers: competitors of your customers, members of the same associations, exhibitors at the same niche events.
2. Same model, adjacent niche: a company selling the same way to a neighbouring market.
3. Same stack and stage: companies running the same tools at the same size.

Direct peers convert best because the customer story transfers word for word.

### 4. Score each match
| Component | Points |
| --- | --- |
| Shares the core niche and model | 0-40 |
| Size and stage within seed range | 0-20 |
| Shares stack or team structure | 0-15 |
| Active trigger in last 90 days | 0-25 |

70+ goes to outbound now; 50-69 goes to a nurture or a later wave.

### 5. Attach the reference
For each account, name the seed customer it most resembles. That becomes the proof point in the first message, if the customer is approved for reference.

## Output format

```
Seeds: <list>  |  Shared traits: <3-5 weighted traits>
Lookalikes (ranked):
  <company> - score - match reasons (2-3) - trigger - closest seed - approved to name? y/n
Excluded: <counts by reason>
```

## What good looks like

- Match reasons a rep could say out loud: "Same model as Northwind: field teams selling into independent pharmacies."
- Direct peers of happy customers lead the list.
- Timing is scored, so the top of the list is not just similar but ready.
- The common mistake is matching on industry and size only, which returns hundreds of generic companies and none of the nuance that made the seeds buy.

## Rules

- MUST explain why each account matched.
- MUST only name a reference customer if the user confirms the customer is approved for that.
- NEVER include current customers, competitors or open deals.

## Example prompts

- "Here are our 12 best customers. Find 100 lookalikes and rank them."
- "Find companies like Northwind and Contoso and tell me which customer story to use for each."
- "Build a lookalike list from our top accounts in healthcare only."

Use this the moment a prospect says yes. Interest fades fast; every extra email of back and forth loses some meetings, and a vague invite causes no-shows.

## Inputs

- The positive reply and thread.
- Availability (2-3 specific slots) or a booking link.
- Meeting purpose and length; who else should attend.

## The play

### 1. Reply fast with two options
Within the hour if possible. Offer two specific times in their time zone, plus the link as a fallback. Choices beat open questions ("When works for you?").

> Great, Maya. 20 minutes on how your close runs and what Contoso changed. Does Tuesday 10:00 or Wednesday 14:00 (your time) work? If neither, pick any time here: <link>

### 2. Send a calendar invite that sells the meeting
- **Title**: "<Their company> + <Your company>: <topic>" (e.g. "Lumen + Acme: month-end close").
- **Description**: three bullet agenda, what they get from it, the video link, and one line on how to reschedule.
- Their time zone in the invite; never assume.

### 3. Confirm in writing
A short confirmation that restates the outcome they will get, and asks one prep question ("Anything specific you want to cover?") which makes them invest in the meeting.

### 4. Remind the day before
A short, useful reminder: the agenda, a relevant one-line insight, the link. Not "just confirming we're still on".

### 5. Handle edge cases
- **Assistant schedules**: give them two slots and the agenda; copy the prospect.
- **Multiple attendees**: ask who else should join and offer to send them a one-line context.
- **Booked 2+ weeks out**: send one value touch in between (a short story or resource) to keep it alive.

## Templates

**Invite description**
```
What we'll cover (20 min):
- How month-end close runs at Lumen today
- What Contoso changed to close in 4 days
- Whether the same approach fits your team
Need to move it? Reply to this invite and I'll find a new time.
```

**Day-before reminder**
> Hi Maya, looking forward to tomorrow at 10. I'll bring the approval checklist Contoso used. Link: <video link>

## What good looks like

- Booked within one or two emails of the yes.
- Invite title and agenda make the value obvious to anyone who sees the calendar.
- Show rate 80%+ for meetings booked within a week.
- The common mistake is "When works for you?", followed by four emails of scheduling while interest cools.

## Rules

- MUST confirm the time zone explicitly.
- MUST send a calendar invite with an agenda and a working video link.
- NEVER book a meeting the prospect did not agree to.
- NEVER add attendees from their company without asking.

## Example prompts

- "They replied 'sure, let's chat next week'. Write the booking reply."
- "Write a calendar invite and confirmation for a discovery call with a CFO."
- "Our show rate is 60%. Fix our confirmation and reminder emails."
skills.html:
Use this the moment a prospect says yes. Interest fades fast; every extra email of back and forth loses some meetings, and a vague invite causes no-shows.

Inputs

  • The positive reply and thread.
  • Availability (2-3 specific slots) or a booking link.
  • Meeting purpose and length; who else should attend.

The play

1. Reply fast with two options

Within the hour if possible. Offer two specific times in their time zone, plus the link as a fallback. Choices beat open questions ("When works for you?").

Great, Maya. 20 minutes on how your close runs and what Contoso changed. Does Tuesday 10:00 or Wednesday 14:00 (your time) work? If neither, pick any time here: <link>

2. Send a calendar invite that sells the meeting

  • Title: "<Their company> + <Your company>: <topic>" (e.g. "Lumen + Acme: month-end close").
  • Description: three bullet agenda, what they get from it, the video link, and one line on how to reschedule.
  • Their time zone in the invite; never assume.

3. Confirm in writing

A short confirmation that restates the outcome they will get, and asks one prep question ("Anything specific you want to cover?") which makes them invest in the meeting.

4. Remind the day before

A short, useful reminder: the agenda, a relevant one-line insight, the link. Not "just confirming we're still on".

5. Handle edge cases

  • Assistant schedules: give them two slots and the agenda; copy the prospect.
  • Multiple attendees: ask who else should join and offer to send them a one-line context.
  • Booked 2+ weeks out: send one value touch in between (a short story or resource) to keep it alive.

Templates

Invite description

What we'll cover (20 min):
- How month-end close runs at Lumen today
- What Contoso changed to close in 4 days
- Whether the same approach fits your team
Need to move it? Reply to this invite and I'll find a new time.

Day-before reminder

Hi Maya, looking forward to tomorrow at 10. I'll bring the approval checklist Contoso used. Link: <video link>

What good looks like

  • Booked within one or two emails of the yes.
  • Invite title and agenda make the value obvious to anyone who sees the calendar.
  • Show rate 80%+ for meetings booked within a week.
  • The common mistake is "When works for you?", followed by four emails of scheduling while interest cools.

Rules

  • MUST confirm the time zone explicitly.
  • MUST send a calendar invite with an agenda and a working video link.
  • NEVER book a meeting the prospect did not agree to.
  • NEVER add attendees from their company without asking.

Example prompts

  • "They replied 'sure, let's chat next week'. Write the booking reply."
  • "Write a calendar invite and confirmation for a discovery call with a CFO."
  • "Our show rate is 60%. Fix our confirmation and reminder emails."

Use this when the same pitch goes to a CFO, a team lead and an engineer. It produces a matrix that keeps the core value proposition but changes the pain, proof and words for each reader.

## Inputs

- The core value proposition and pillars.
- Personas (economic buyer, champion, user, technical evaluator).
- Proof points, tagged by what they prove.

## The play

### 1. Build the grid
Rows are personas; columns are:

| Column | What goes in |
| --- | --- |
| Measured on | The metric they own |
| Top pain | The pain in their words |
| Outcome | The result they want |
| Pillar to lead with | Which of your pillars fits best |
| Proof | The proof point that persuades this role |
| Objection | Their most likely pushback and the answer |
| Use | Words that resonate |
| Avoid | Words that make them tune out |

### 2. Pick the lead pillar per persona
A CFO hears cost and risk; a team lead hears time and quality; an engineer hears how it works and what it touches. Same product, different first sentence.

### 3. Write the lines
Per persona: an email opener, a LinkedIn opener, a 20-second call opener and a landing page headline. Lines reuse the matrix words exactly.

### 4. Add industry or stage variants only when they change the pain
A variant earns a row when the pain or the proof genuinely differs (healthcare compliance, a seed-stage team without a RevOps person). Otherwise, the persona row is enough.

## Example row

| Persona | Measured on | Top pain | Outcome | Lead pillar | Proof | Objection → answer | Use | Avoid |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CFO | Close time, audit findings, headcount cost | "We hire analysts to do reconciliation" | 5-day close without new hires | Automation of reconciliation | Contoso: 9 → 4 days, one analyst redeployed | "Another tool to buy" → replaces 2 tools and manual hours | close, audit trail, headcount | revolutionary, synergy, seamless |

Lines for the CFO:
- Email: "Most finance teams your size close in 8-10 days, and most of it is reconciliation."
- Call: "I work with CFOs who'd rather not hire another analyst to get to a 5-day close."
- Landing page: "A 5-day close, without another analyst."

## What good looks like

- Every persona row has a different first sentence.
- Proof is matched to persona.
- The matrix fits on one page; reps actually use it.
- The common mistake is building a 12-column matrix for 15 micro-segments that nobody opens again.

## Rules

- MUST keep the core value proposition consistent across rows.
- MUST use only approved proof points.
- NEVER create rows for segments without distinct pains.

## Example prompts

- "Build a messaging matrix for CFO, Controller and AP Manager from our value prop."
- "Our SDRs use the same pitch for everyone. Create persona lines for email and LinkedIn."
- "Add healthcare and fintech variants to our messaging matrix where they truly differ."

Use this when one channel is not enough. Prospects who see you in two or three places in a short window remember you; the trick is making the touches feel like one conversation rather than an ambush.

## Inputs

- Persona and tier.
- Channels available and the sender's capacity per day on each.
- Offer, proof and the campaign's central problem.

## The play

### 1. Choose channels by persona
| Persona | Lead channel | Support channels |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Founders, small companies | LinkedIn | Email |
| Sales and marketing leaders | LinkedIn and email | Video |
| Finance, operations, IT | Email | Phone |
| Field and frontline managers | Phone | Email, text where lawful and consented |
| Enterprise executives | Email via champion or referral | LinkedIn, direct mail |

### 2. Scale effort by tier
- **Tier 1**: 10-14 touches over 3-4 weeks, 3-4 channels, 1:1 personalization.
- **Tier 2**: 7-9 touches over 3 weeks, 2-3 channels, segment copy plus a personal line.
- **Tier 3**: 4-6 touches over 2-3 weeks, 1-2 channels, segment copy.

### 3. Order the touches
Start where trust is cheapest: a LinkedIn profile view or connection request before the first email makes the email's sender name familiar. Calls work best right after an email ("I sent you a note on Tuesday about..."). Read [references/cadence-templates.md](references/cadence-templates.md) for day-by-day templates per tier.

### 4. Thread the story
Every touch references the same problem from a new angle: the email names the problem, the LinkedIn message asks a question about it, the call follows up on the email, the video shows a 30-second example.

### 5. Plan capacity
Count touches per day per sender across all active prospects. A Tier 1 cadence for 50 new accounts a week can mean 80+ tasks a day; cut the number of new accounts before cutting quality.

### 6. Exit rules
Any reply on any channel stops every automated step on every channel. Bookings at the account stop all cadences at that account.

## What good looks like

- A prospect who replies says "I saw your note on LinkedIn too", not "why are you messaging me everywhere?".
- Channel order makes each touch easier: connection, then email, then call referencing the email.
- Task load per rep is realistic and finished daily.
- The common mistake is running separate email and LinkedIn campaigns that each think they own the prospect, sending two unrelated first messages on the same day.

## Rules

- MUST stop all channels on a reply in any channel.
- MUST keep each channel inside its safe daily limits.
- MUST respect calling and texting consent rules for the region.
- NEVER send the same message copy across channels.

## Example prompts

- "Build a 3-week multichannel cadence for Tier 1 CFO accounts: email, LinkedIn and phone."
- "We have email and LinkedIn only. Design Tier 2 and Tier 3 cadences."
- "How many new accounts a week can 2 SDRs handle on this cadence?"

references.title: Cadence templates
references.markdown:
# Cadence templates

## Tier 1: 21 days, 12 touches

| Day | Channel | Touch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | LinkedIn | View profile; engage with a recent post if relevant |
| 1 | LinkedIn | Connection request, note on the shared topic |
| 2 | Email | Email 1: observation → problem → proof → ask |
| 4 | Phone | Call 1, referencing email 1; voicemail if no answer |
| 4 | Email | Short reply to email 1: "Left you a voicemail about..." |
| 6 | LinkedIn | Message 1 (if accepted): question on the topic |
| 8 | Email | Email 2: new angle, value add |
| 10 | Video | 45-60 second personal video on their situation |
| 12 | Phone | Call 2 |
| 15 | Email | Email 3: customer story (new thread) |
| 17 | LinkedIn | Message 2: share a resource |
| 21 | Email | Break-up email |

## Tier 2: 18 days, 8 touches

| Day | Channel | Touch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | LinkedIn | Connection request |
| 2 | Email | Email 1 |
| 5 | Email | Email 2 (same thread) |
| 6 | LinkedIn | Message 1 (if accepted) |
| 9 | Phone | Call (optional by persona) |
| 11 | Email | Email 3 (new thread, proof) |
| 14 | LinkedIn | Message 2 |
| 18 | Email | Break-up email |

## Tier 3: 14 days, 5 touches

| Day | Channel | Touch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Email | Email 1 |
| 4 | Email | Email 2 |
| 5 | LinkedIn | Connection request |
| 9 | Email | Email 3 |
| 14 | Email | Break-up |

## Daily task math

Tasks per day ≈ new accounts per day × contacts per account × touches per contact ÷ cadence length in days × overlap factor (≈1.0 once running).

Example: 4 Tier 1 accounts a day × 2 contacts × 12 touches ÷ 21 days ≈ 4.6 tasks per day per new-account batch; at steady state with three weeks of overlap, about 100 tasks a day. Too many for one rep alongside calls, so drop to 2-3 new Tier 1 accounts a day.

## Cross-channel copy thread

- Email 1: "Teams your size usually lose a week a month to approvals."
- Call: "I sent you a note Tuesday about approvals eating the last week of the month. Is that true for your team?"
- LinkedIn: "Curious, does your close slow down at approvals or at reconciliation?"
- Video: 45 seconds walking through how a peer set a day-3 approval cut-off.

Use this once a buyer agrees the problem is worth solving. A shared plan turns "we'll get back to you" into dated steps both sides own, and shows early whether the close date is real.

## Inputs

- The buyer's target date for value (go-live, a launch, a quarter start) and why it matters.
- What is known about their decision and paper process.
- Stakeholders on both sides.

## The play

### 1. Anchor on their date
Start from the date the buyer needs results, not your quarter end. "To have reps using it by 1 March, onboarding starts 1 February, so signature by 25 January."

### 2. List every step, both sides
Evaluation, stakeholder meetings, technical review, security questionnaire, legal review, procurement and vendor setup, budget approval, signature, kickoff, onboarding milestones. Most slipped deals slip on steps nobody listed. Read [references/map-template.md](references/map-template.md) for the template and typical durations.

### 3. Assign owners and dates
Every step has a named owner (buyer or seller side) and a date. Steps without a buyer-side owner are wishes.

### 4. Mark the critical path
The longest chain of dependent steps, usually security plus legal plus procurement. Start them in parallel and early.

### 5. Introduce it as help
Send the plan to the champion as a tool for their internal process: "Here's a draft of what usually needs to happen; what did I miss?" Let them edit it. A plan the buyer has changed is a plan they own.

### 6. Review it every week
Update status, move dates honestly, and raise slips early.

## Champion email

> Hi Priya, to hit reps live by 1 March, I sketched the steps that usually need to happen on both sides (attached). Some I've guessed, especially security and procurement at Lumen. Could you fix what's wrong and add anything I missed? Happy to walk through it on Thursday's call.

## What good looks like

- The buyer edits the plan, adds steps and owns dates.
- Security, legal and procurement start before the final presentation, not after.
- The plan continues past signature into the first value milestone, which keeps the conversation about outcomes.
- The common mistake is a seller-only checklist sent as an ultimatum the week before quarter end.

## Rules

- MUST anchor dates on the buyer's goal.
- MUST name an owner for every step.
- NEVER invent deadlines or artificial urgency in the plan.

## Example prompts

- "Build a mutual action plan for our $60k deal with Lumen; they want reps live by 1 March."
- "This deal keeps slipping. Turn my notes into a close plan with the critical path."
- "Write the email that introduces the plan to our champion."

Use this when a meeting is missed. Most no-shows are not rejections: calendars collide, days get away. A gracious, fast follow-up rebooks a large share of them.

## Inputs

- Meeting details: who, when, purpose, how it was booked.
- The thread before the meeting.
- How many times they have rescheduled already.

## The play

### 1. Wait five to ten minutes, then reach out once
At five minutes past: a short email ("I'm on the line; no worries if today got away from you"). If the person's phone number is known and calling is appropriate, one call.

### 2. Same day: rebook without guilt
> Hi Maya, no problem at all about today. I know how quarter-end weeks go. Would Thursday 10:00 or Friday 14:00 work instead? Or pick any time here: <link>

### 3. Day 2-3: add value
If no answer, send something useful tied to the meeting topic (the checklist, the short customer story), plus the link.

### 4. Day 6-7: close the loop
> Hi Maya, I'll take this off my list for now. If month-end close gets back on the agenda, reply "close" and I'll send times.

Optionally, one LinkedIn message between steps 3 and 4 if connected.

### 5. Second no-show
After two missed meetings, do not offer a third slot directly. Ask whether the topic is still a priority; if yes, ask them to pick a time.

### 6. Diagnose patterns
| Pattern | Likely cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No-shows on meetings booked 2+ weeks out | Interest fades | Book within 7 days; add a value touch in between |
| No-shows after links with no agenda | Unclear value | Agenda in invite; confirmation with a prep question |
| High no-shows from one campaign | Weak qualification or a pushy ask | Fix the ask; qualify before booking |
| No-shows at certain times | Time zone errors, Monday mornings, Friday afternoons | Confirm zones; avoid those slots |

## What good looks like

- First message within 15 minutes of the missed start time.
- Rebook rate of 30-50% on first-time no-shows.
- The common mistake is the passive-aggressive "Sorry we missed you, I waited 15 minutes", which makes rebooking awkward.

## Rules

- MUST keep the tone gracious, every time.
- MUST stop after the close-the-loop message unless they reply.
- NEVER charge, threaten or shame a no-show.
- NEVER escalate to their manager because they missed a sales meeting.

## Example prompts

- "My 2pm with the VP of Ops didn't show. Write the follow-up sequence."
- "This prospect has rescheduled twice. What now?"
- "Our no-show rate is 35%. Diagnose and fix our booking process."

Use this when a buyer pushes back. Most objections are questions in disguise; the response that works first finds out which question.

## Inputs

- The objection, in the buyer's exact words.
- Context: cold reply, discovery call, late-stage deal; who said it.
- Proof available: customer stories, numbers, documents.

## The play

### 1. Diagnose before answering
| Surface objection | Often really means |
| --- | --- |
| "Too expensive" | Value not clear yet, wrong package, budget timing, or a competitor quote |
| "We already have a solution" | Switching feels risky; current pain not acknowledged |
| "Not a priority" | Problem not tied to something they are measured on |
| "Send me some info" | Polite exit, or genuinely busy |
| "I need to talk to my team" | Not the decision-maker, or not convinced enough to champion |
| "We tried something like this" | Past failure; fear of repeating it |

### 2. Choose the pattern
- **Clarify**: ask a question that surfaces the real concern. Default first move.
- **Reframe**: change the comparison (cost of the problem vs the price; risk of doing nothing).
- **Prove**: a peer who had the same concern and what happened.
- **Defer**: agree a specific later moment when the condition changes.
- **Walk away**: when the objection reveals a genuine bad fit, say so. It builds trust and saves time.

### 3. Write the response
Acknowledge in a few words (no "I totally understand"), then the pattern. Keep email responses under 80 words. On calls, ask and then stop talking.

Read [references/objection-library.md](references/objection-library.md) for responses to the 12 most common B2B objections, by stage.

### 4. Log it
Every objection goes into the library with the response that worked. Patterns across deals feed messaging and product.

## What good looks like

- The first response is usually a question.
- Proof matches the objection: a security concern gets a security document, not a ROI story.
- Bad-fit objections are accepted, not "overcome".
- The common mistake is arguing: answering a price objection with a list of features.

## Rules

- MUST clarify before rebutting when the real concern is unclear.
- MUST use only approved proof points and real pricing.
- NEVER pressure with fake deadlines or "this price ends Friday" unless it is true.
- NEVER disparage a competitor the buyer uses.

## Example prompts

- "Prospect replied 'we're happy with our current vendor'. Draft a response."
- "Build an objection library for our sales team from these 20 call notes."
- "On calls I freeze at 'it's too expensive'. Give me a talk track."

references.title: Objection library
references.markdown:
# Objection library

## Early stage (cold replies, first calls)

| Objection | Response |
| --- | --- |
| "Not interested." | "Fair enough. Is that because <problem> isn't an issue for you, or just not a priority right now?" |
| "We already use <tool>." | "Good to know. How is it handling <specific weak spot>? If it's working, I'll leave you be." |
| "Send me some info." | "Happy to. So it's relevant: are you mostly looking at <outcome A> or <outcome B>?" |
| "No budget." | "Makes sense. When does planning start for next year? I'd rather be useful then." |
| "Not the right person." | "Thanks. Who owns <problem> on your team?" |
| "Bad timing." | "When would be better, and what changes then?" Book the date. |

## Mid stage (discovery, demo)

| Objection | Response |
| --- | --- |
| "Too expensive." | "Compared to what? ... What does <problem> cost you today in hours or lost deals?" Then show the maths with their numbers. |
| "We tried something like this and it failed." | "What happened? ... The two most common reasons are <x> and <y>; here's how <peer> avoided them." |
| "I need to talk to my team." | "Of course. Who's involved, and what will they ask you that I can help answer? Want me to join for 15 minutes?" |
| "We'll build it ourselves." | "Could be the right call. How many engineering weeks, and what does maintaining it cost per year?" |

## Late stage (proposal, procurement)

| Objection | Response |
| --- | --- |
| "Your competitor is cheaper." | "They may be. Can we compare line by line? Teams usually find the difference in <onboarding, limits, support>. If they're a better fit, I'll tell you." |
| "Security has concerns." | "Which ones? I'll send the security pack today and can set up a call with our security lead this week." |
| "Can you do a bigger discount?" | Trade, don't give: "I can look at that if we can <sign by date / commit annually / be a reference>." |
| "Legal needs more time." | "Understood. Which clauses? We have pre-approved alternatives for the common ones." |

## Proof matching

| Concern type | Best proof |
| --- | --- |
| Value | Peer result with numbers; their own maths |
| Risk of switching | Migration plan, timeline, a reference who switched |
| Security and compliance | Documents, certifications, data-flow diagram |
| Adoption | Usage numbers from a similar team, onboarding plan |
| Price | Cost-of-problem calculation, packaging options |

Use this to run outbound tests that produce decisions. Most outbound "tests" compare 40 sends to 40 sends and crown a winner by noise.

## Inputs

- The current campaign and its baseline numbers.
- The metric to improve (usually positive reply rate or meetings per 100 contacts).
- How many contacts per week the team can send to the test.

## The play

### 1. Test the biggest lever first
Impact order, roughly: **list and segment** > **angle and offer** > **first line and personalization** > **CTA** > **subject line** > **send time**. Testing send time while the list is wrong wastes a month.

### 2. Write a hypothesis
"Leading with the hiring trigger instead of the pain will raise positive replies for SDR leaders, because the trigger shows why now." One variable changes; everything else stays the same.

### 3. Size it
Required contacts per variant depend on baseline and the lift you want to detect:

| Baseline positive reply rate | Detect 2x lift | Detect 1.5x lift |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1% | ~2,300 per variant | ~7,700 per variant |
| 2% | ~1,150 | ~3,800 |
| 4% | ~550 | ~1,900 |

(Approximate, 80% power, 5% significance.) Rare outcomes need big samples. If volume cannot reach the size, test bigger changes (detect 2x), use total reply rate as a leading metric (it has a higher baseline), or run the test across several weeks of sends.

### 4. Split fairly
Random assignment within the same segment, same senders spread across both variants, same days and times. Never run variant A this week and B next week.

### 5. Decide in advance
Write the stop rule: the sample size, the metric, and what counts as a win. Check for guardrails too: bounce and unsubscribe rates must not rise.

### 6. Read and log
Report both variants with counts, the difference and whether it clears the rule. "No difference" is a result: keep the cheaper or simpler variant. Log every test so the team does not re-run old ones.

## Output format

```
Test: <name>   Hypothesis: <...>
Variable: <one>   Held constant: <list, senders, timing, steps>
Metric: <primary> | Guardrails: bounces, opt-outs
Size: N per variant | Expected duration: N weeks
Decision rule: <...>
Readout: A x/N (x%) vs B x/N (x%) → winner / no difference → action
```

## What good looks like

- One variable per test.
- Sample size decided before launch.
- The log shows what was learned, including tests that changed nothing.
- The common mistake is judging on open rates, which are inflated by privacy features and say nothing about replies.

## Rules

- MUST change only one variable per test.
- MUST set sample size and decision rule before launch.
- NEVER declare a winner below the planned sample, and never on fewer than 200 contacts per variant.
- NEVER use open rate as the deciding metric.

## Example prompts

- "Design a test: trigger-led vs pain-led first email for VP Sales. We send 400 a week."
- "Here are results for two variants. Is B really better?"
- "Plan the next 3 outbound experiments for our team, in order of impact."

Use this when setting targets or headcount. It shows what a number actually requires, and which conversion rate to improve before adding people.

## Inputs

- Target: new revenue (or pipeline) for the period, and how much should come from outbound.
- Rates: win rate, average deal size, held meeting to opportunity, booked to held, positive reply to booked, positive reply rate per contact. Measured if possible; otherwise labelled assumptions.
- Team: SDRs and AEs, and their realistic capacity.

## The play

### 1. Run the reverse funnel
```
Outbound revenue target              $600,000 per quarter
÷ average deal size ($20,000)        = 30 deals won
÷ win rate (25%)                     = 120 opportunities
÷ meeting → opportunity (50%)        = 240 meetings held
÷ show rate (80%)                    = 300 meetings booked
÷ positive reply → booked (60%)      = 500 positive replies
÷ positive reply rate (1.5%)         = 33,333 contacts per quarter
÷ 13 weeks                           = 2,564 new contacts per week
```

### 2. Convert to daily activity
Contacts per week × touches per contact ÷ 5 = touches per day across the team. Divide by reps for activity per rep, and compare with what one rep can do well (for example 50-80 new contacts a week with personalization).

### 3. Check headcount and capacity
Reps needed = contacts per week ÷ realistic contacts per rep per week. AEs needed = meetings per week ÷ meetings one AE can hold well (typically 8-15).

### 4. Check market size
Contacts per year vs reachable contacts in the ICP. If the plan needs 130,000 contacts a year and the ICP has 25,000, the plan is impossible as written.

### 5. Show the levers
Recalculate with each rate improved by a realistic step. Usually positive reply rate and meeting-to-opportunity rate change the answer most. Example: 1.5% → 2.5% positive replies cuts required contacts by 40%.

## Output format

```
Target → deals → opportunities → meetings held → booked → positive replies → contacts
Per week: contacts N | touches N | per rep N
Headcount: SDRs N (have N) | AEs N (have N)
Market check: N contacts/year vs N reachable → OK / exhausts in N months
Levers: <rate change → contacts needed>
Assumptions: <which rates are measured vs assumed>
```

## What good looks like

- Every rate is labelled measured or assumed.
- The plan is checked against both capacity and market size.
- The answer recommends the lever to improve before the hire to make.
- The common mistake is solving a target with activity alone ("send 3x more"), which burns the market and the domains.

## Rules

- MUST label assumed rates and use conservative ones.
- MUST check the plan against the reachable market.
- NEVER present the output as a forecast; it is a requirement model.

## Example prompts

- "We need $1.2M in new ARR from outbound this year. What activity does that take?"
- "How many SDRs do we need for 200 meetings a quarter?"
- "Which conversion rate should we improve first to hit target without hiring?"

---

Use this weekly or before a forecast call. It turns a pipeline export into an honest forecast and a short list of actions that move the number.

## Inputs

- Pipeline export: deal, owner, stage, amount, close date, created date, last activity, next step, contacts.
- Quota or target for the period and what has closed so far.
- Historical stage conversion rates if available.

## The play

### 1. Check coverage
Open pipeline due this period ÷ remaining target. Healthy coverage depends on win rate; at a 25% win rate, 3-4x is typical. Read [references/pipeline-health.md](references/pipeline-health.md) for the health checks, thresholds and the risk scoring table.

### 2. Run the health checks
- **Aging**: deals in a stage longer than 1.5x the average for that stage.
- **Slips**: close date moved 2+ times.
- **No next step**: no future activity scheduled.
- **Stale**: no activity in 14+ days.
- **Single-threaded**: one contact engaged.
- **Close date in the past**.
- **Stage mismatch**: proposal stage without an economic buyer met.

### 3. Score deal risk
Each failing check adds risk points. High-risk deals in commit move to best case or out, with the reason.

### 4. Build the forecast
| Category | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Commit | Low risk, verbal yes or clear paper process, close date backed by a plan |
| Best case | Medium risk, strong engagement, one open gap |
| Upside | Early or high risk |
| Remove | Dead, past due with no response, or no next step for 30 days |

Weighted forecast = commit + (best case × historical conversion).

### 5. Choose the actions
Three to five actions that change the quarter: a deal that needs an executive call, a stalled proposal, a missing champion, pipeline generation if coverage is short.

## Output format

```
Target: X | Closed: X | Gap: X | Coverage: Nx (healthy / thin)
Forecast: Commit X | Best case X | Upside X | Weighted X
Risks: <deal - risk score - failing checks - recommendation>
Actions this week: <action - owner - expected impact>
Pipeline hygiene: N deals with past close dates, N without next steps
```

## What good looks like

- Every deal moved out of commit has a stated reason.
- The forecast says what would need to be true for best case to land.
- Actions are specific, owned and dated.
- The common mistake is reviewing deals by amount only; a small deal with a signed order form matters more for the forecast than a big deal with no economic buyer.

## Rules

- MUST base risk on evidence (activity, dates, contacts), not on rep confidence.
- MUST flag past-due close dates and missing next steps.
- NEVER change records in the CRM without approval; propose updates instead.

## Example prompts

- "Here's our pipeline export. Prep me for Monday's forecast call."
- "Which of my 30 open deals are most at risk this quarter?"
- "We need $400k more this quarter. Is the pipeline enough, and what should we do?"

references.title: Pipeline health checks
references.markdown:
# Pipeline health checks

## Coverage targets by win rate

| Win rate (created to won) | Healthy coverage |
| --- | --- |
| 15% | 5-6x |
| 20% | 4-5x |
| 25% | 3-4x |
| 33% | 2.5-3x |

Coverage counts only deals with close dates inside the period and stages past discovery.

## Risk scoring

| Check | Risk points |
| --- | --- |
| Close date moved 2+ times | 3 |
| No activity in 14+ days | 3 |
| No next step scheduled | 2 |
| Single-threaded | 2 |
| Economic buyer not met (proposal stage or later) | 3 |
| Aging: 1.5x+ average time in stage | 2 |
| Close date in the past | 3 |
| Champion not tested | 1 |
| Competitor preferred by buyer (stated) | 2 |

Risk: 0-2 low, 3-5 medium, 6+ high.

## Stage conversion sanity check

| Stage | Typical win probability (calibrate with your data) |
| --- | --- |
| Discovery | 10-15% |
| Evaluation | 25-35% |
| Proposal | 40-55% |
| Negotiation / verbal | 65-80% |
| Commit with paper process underway | 85-95% |

If the team's commit category historically closes below 80%, the commit rules are too loose.

## Weekly review flow (30 minutes)

1. Numbers: target, closed, gap, coverage (5 min).
2. Commit deals: confirm each with evidence (10 min).
3. Best-case deals: what moves them to commit (10 min).
4. Hygiene and pipeline creation: past dates, missing next steps, new pipeline needed (5 min).

Use this when a post has drawn reactions and comments from people who might be buyers. Engagement shows interest in a topic; the follow-up continues that topic and lets the conversation find the business problem.

## Inputs

- The engagers: name, title, company, and how they engaged (reaction, comment, share).
- The post: author, topic and the point it made.
- The ICP.

## The play

### 1. Filter hard
Typically 70-90% of engagers are outside any ICP: peers, vendors, recruiters, job seekers, friends. Keep only ICP fits. Remove competitors and current customers (route customers to the account owner instead).

### 2. Rank by engagement strength
| Engagement | Strength |
| --- | --- |
| Thoughtful comment adding a view or a question | Strongest |
| Share with their own commentary | Strong |
| Short comment ("Great post!") | Medium |
| Reaction only | Weak |
| Engaged with two or more posts on the topic in 30 days | Boost one level |

### 3. Decide the source angle
- **Your own or your team's post**: you can reference it directly; they engaged with you.
- **Someone else's post** (an industry voice, a competitor): reference the topic, not the fact you saw their reaction. Keep it light.

### 4. Write the follow-up
Connection note: 1-2 sentences continuing the topic. After they accept: a question that bridges the topic to their situation. No pitch until they show the problem is real for them.

> Connection note: "Your comment about ramp being a data problem stuck with me. Would be good to have you in my network."
>
> After accepting: "Curious how you handle that at Lumen. Do new reps build their own lists, or does someone hand them accounts on day one?"

## What good looks like

- Under 25% of engagers make it through the filter. If 80% do, the filter is too loose.
- Messages reference the idea in the post, not the act of liking it.
- Commenters get a personal reference to what they actually said.
- The common mistake is mass-messaging every reaction with "Thanks for liking my post! Want a demo?"

## Rules

- MUST filter engagers against the ICP before writing.
- MUST stay within daily LinkedIn activity limits.
- NEVER pitch in the connection note.
- NEVER say you saw someone react to a third party's post.

## Example prompts

- "Here are 140 people who engaged with our founder's post on SDR ramp. Who should we reach out to and with what?"
- "Write connection notes for the 12 commenters who fit our ICP."
- "Turn engagers on this competitor's post into a warm outreach list."
