skills.name: proposal-follow-up
skills.title: Proposal follow-up
skills.description: Use this skill when a proposal or quote has been sent and the buyer has gone quiet or is stalling: "follow up on my proposal", "they have the quote but no decision", "proposal stuck in review". Diagnoses where the deal is really stuck (economic buyer, budget, competitor, priority, procurement, champion), writes a follow-up sequence that addresses that cause with value instead of nagging, and sets the point to escalate or close the opportunity.
skills.summary: Use this when a proposal sits unanswered. Silence after a proposal almost always has a specific cause; following up on the cause works better than asking "any updates?".
skills.markdown:
---
name: proposal-follow-up
description: "Use this skill when a proposal or quote has been sent and the buyer has gone quiet or is stalling: \"follow up on my proposal\", \"they have the quote but no decision\", \"proposal stuck in review\". Diagnoses where the deal is really stuck (economic buyer, budget, competitor, priority, procurement, champion), writes a follow-up sequence that addresses that cause with value instead of nagging, and sets the point to escalate or close the opportunity."
license: MIT
metadata:
  title: Proposal follow-up
  category: deals
  tags: "Sales, Founders, Agencies"
  author: prosyo
  version: "1.0.0"
  keywords: "proposal follow up email, follow up after sending quote, stalled deal email, claude proposal follow up skill, sales proposal no response"
  inputs: "Proposal and date sent, Deal notes, Stakeholders"
  outputs: "Stall diagnosis, Follow-up sequence, Escalation and close plan"
---

Use this when a proposal sits unanswered. Silence after a proposal almost always has a specific cause; following up on the cause works better than asking "any updates?".

## Inputs

- The proposal: what, how much, when sent, any deadline in it.
- Deal notes: who saw it, who decides, competitors, what was promised.
- Stakeholders and the champion's last message.

## The play

### 1. Diagnose the stall
| Clue | Likely cause | Follow-up angle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Champion silent, was engaged before | Lost internal fight or priority shift | Ask directly, offer help with the internal case |
| "Reviewing with the team" for 2+ weeks | Economic buyer not convinced or not involved | Offer a short call with the economic buyer |
| Questions about price only | Budget gap or competitor quote | Options: phasing, packaging, terms |
| Procurement or legal mentioned | Paper process | Offer documents and pre-approved terms |
| Nothing since the demo went poorly | Fit concern | Address the concern or offer a focused trial |

### 2. Sequence (over 2-3 weeks)
1. **Day 3-5**: value plus a question about the cause: a one-page business case built from their numbers, and "What questions came up when you shared it?"
2. **Day 8-10**: address the likely blocker: options for price, security documents, or an offer to join the internal meeting.
3. **Day 14-16**: multi-thread: a short note to another stakeholder you have met, adding value, not going around the champion.
4. **Day 21**: honest check-in with a multiple-choice question, or close the opportunity.

### 3. Escalate with care
Executive-to-executive outreach works when there was real engagement and the deal is meaningful. Frame it as a check on how the evaluation is going, never as pressure.

### 4. Decide when to close
If three touches over three weeks get nothing, mark the deal lost to "no decision" and move to nurture. An honest pipeline beats a hopeful one.

## Example

> Hi Priya, I put your numbers into a one-page case for the CFO: 5 days saved a month, about $480k a year at your volumes, against a $60k cost. Feel free to edit it before sharing. What questions came up when you discussed the proposal with the team?

## What good looks like

- Every follow-up contains something the buyer can use internally.
- The diagnosis drives the angle; price follow-ups do not go to a champion whose problem is the economic buyer.
- The common mistake is "Just checking in on the proposal" five times, then an unrequested discount.

## Rules

- MUST diagnose the stall before writing.
- MUST keep the champion informed before contacting other stakeholders.
- NEVER offer an unrequested discount as a follow-up tactic.
- NEVER invent an expiring offer.

## Example prompts

- "Sent the proposal 12 days ago, no reply from our champion. Diagnose and write the follow-ups."
- "They said 'reviewing internally' three weeks ago. What now?"
- "Build a business case one-pager from our discovery numbers to send as a follow-up."

Use this for one person you are about to contact or meet. It produces a brief a rep can read in 60 seconds and a first line that proves the message was written for them.

## Inputs

- Name, company and title, plus a profile link if available.
- Your offer and the persona this person maps to.
- Any CRM history with this person or their company.

## The play

### 1. Confirm the person
Check they still work at the company and in the role. Roughly one in five B2B contacts changes jobs each year; a brief about the wrong job is wasted.

### 2. Gather in this order
1. Their own words: posts, comments, articles, podcast or event appearances from the last 6 months.
2. Career path: previous companies and roles, tenure in this role. A person 60 days into a role behaves differently from one 4 years in.
3. Company context: one or two triggers from the account level that land on their desk.
4. Shared ground: same former employer, same community, same school, a mutual customer. Use only if real and relevant.

### 3. Rank the hooks
Score each hook on two questions: is it specific to this person, and does it connect to the problem you solve? Keep only hooks that pass both. Read [references/hook-ranking.md](references/hook-ranking.md) for the ranking grid and examples of strong and weak hooks.

### 4. Write the openers
One for email, one for LinkedIn. One or two sentences each, built from the strongest hook, ending in a natural bridge to the problem, not to your product.

## Output format

```
Person: <name> - <title> at <company> - <tenure in role>
Confirmed current: yes/no (source)
Measured on: <likely metrics for the role>
What they talk about: <2-3 themes with links>
Hooks (ranked):
  1. <hook> - <source> - <why it connects>
  2. ...
Email opener: <1-2 sentences>
LinkedIn opener: <1-2 sentences, more conversational>
Avoid: <topics or claims to stay away from>
```

## What good looks like

- The opener could not be sent to anyone else. Swap the name and it breaks.
- It references their thinking, not their resume. "Loved your post" is weak; "your point that SDR ramp is a data problem, not a training problem" is strong.
- When nothing specific exists, the brief says so and falls back to a role-and-trigger opener instead of inventing intimacy.
- The common mistake is personalising on trivia (alma mater, hometown, a sports team) that has nothing to do with the reason for the message.

## Rules

- MUST confirm the person's current role before writing.
- MUST attach a source to every hook.
- NEVER use personal life details: family, health, location history, photos.
- NEVER claim to have read or watched something you did not.
- NEVER mention tracking data such as profile views or website visits in the opener.

## Example prompts

- "Research Priya Shah, VP Revenue at Lumen. Write an email and a LinkedIn opener."
- "I meet Tom Becker tomorrow. Give me a 60-second brief."
- "Find a real hook for each of these 15 prospects, or tell me when there isn't one."

references.title: Hook ranking
references.markdown:
# Hook ranking

## The grid

| | Connects to your problem | Does not connect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Specific to the person** | Use it. Lead with it. | Use only as a light aside, never as the opener. |
| **Generic (role or company level)** | Use when nothing better exists. | Drop it. |

## Hook strength, strongest first

1. **Their stated opinion on the problem you solve.** A post, a talk, a quote in an article.
2. **A change in their remit.** New role, new team, new region, new target.
3. **A project they are visibly running.** Hiring for it, posting about it, speaking about it.
4. **A company trigger that lands on their desk.** Funding with growth targets for a VP Sales.
5. **A peer comparison.** A similar company solved this; name it only if the claim is approved.
6. **Role-level insight.** What people in their role usually wrestle with at their company's stage.

## Strong and weak versions

| Weak | Strong |
| --- | --- |
| "Loved your recent post!" | "Your post on cutting ramp time to 45 days made a point I rarely see: that most of it is list quality, not coaching." |
| "Congrats on the new role!" | "Three months into running RevOps at Lumen is usually when the tool audit starts." |
| "I see you went to Michigan." | (Drop it unless the message is about Michigan.) |
| "Saw you're hiring." | "Four SDR listings in two weeks, all mentioning outbound from scratch, suggests the team is being rebuilt." |

## When there is nothing

About a third of prospects have no public activity. Do not fake it. Use the role-and-trigger fallback:

"Most heads of operations at multi-site groups your size tell us payroll closes take two to three days. Is that true at Northwind too?"

It is honest, it is relevant and it invites a correction, which is still a reply.

Use this to turn goodwill into introductions. Most people are happy to refer; they just need a specific ask and an easy way to do it.

## Inputs

- Customers or contacts who are happy (recent results, good feedback, renewals).
- Target accounts or roles you want to reach, and any known connections.
- Recent wins to reference.

## The play

### 1. Ask at the right moment
Right after a visible win: a result they shared, a renewal, a great review, a successful rollout, a thank-you message from them. Not during an open support issue.

### 2. Make the ask specific
"Do you know anyone who might need this?" gets "I'll think about it." Instead, name two or three companies or a precise role: "I noticed you're connected to Dev at Lumen and know the ops team at Fabrikam. Would either be open to a short intro?"

### 3. Use a double opt-in
Ask the referrer to check with their contact first, so the introduction is welcome. Offer to send a forwardable blurb.

### 4. Write the forwardable blurb
Three or four sentences the referrer can paste: who you are, what you did for them, why it might matter to the contact, and an easy next step. Written in the referrer's voice, short enough to forward from a phone.

> Dev, thought of you: Sam at Acme helped us cut month-end close from 9 days to 4. Given your new entities at Lumen, might be worth 20 minutes. Happy to connect you if useful.

### 5. Follow up and thank
Reply to the introduction within hours, move the referrer to bcc, and tell them what happened afterwards. Thank them whatever the outcome; a handwritten note or a small, appropriate gesture works. Follow any rules their company has about gifts, and disclose referral rewards.

## Templates

**The ask**
> Hi Priya, really glad the 4-day close held through quarter end. One favour: you mentioned knowing the finance lead at Fabrikam. Would they be open to an intro? I've drafted a short note below you could forward if they are. No pressure at all if it's not a fit.

**Thank-you after an intro**
> Priya, thank you for connecting me with Lena. We've got a call next week. I'll let you know how it goes, and I owe you one.

## What good looks like

- Asks name specific people or companies.
- The referrer spends under a minute.
- Every referrer hears back about the outcome.
- The common mistake is a quarterly mass email asking all customers for "any referrals", which almost never produces introductions.

## Rules

- MUST use double opt-in introductions.
- MUST disclose any referral reward and respect the referrer's company policies.
- NEVER contact someone claiming a referral that has not happened.
- NEVER ask a customer with an open problem for a referral.

## Example prompts

- "Priya just renewed and shared great results. Write a referral ask for two specific companies."
- "Write a forwardable blurb for our customers to send to peers."
- "Design a simple customer referral program for a B2B SaaS."

Use this when replies arrive from a campaign. Speed decides how many positive replies become meetings: interested prospects answered within an hour book far more often than those answered the next day.

## Inputs

- Each reply with the message it answers.
- Offer, a booking link or the sender's availability, and approved answers to common questions.
- Who approves outgoing replies.

## The play

### 1. Classify every reply
| Class | Signal | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Interested | "Sure", "Tell me more", "Let's talk", asks for times | Now |
| Question | Asks about price, how it works, integrations | Now |
| Referral | "Talk to Sam" | Today |
| Objection | "We already use X", "No budget", "Not a fit because..." | Today |
| Not now | "Reach out in Q3", "Busy until after launch" | Today, then schedule |
| Not interested | "No thanks", "Not interested" | Today, close politely |
| Wrong person | "I don't handle this" | Today, ask who does |
| Out of office | Auto-reply | Pause; resume after return date |
| Unsubscribe or hostile | "Remove me", "Stop" | Now: suppress everywhere |

Read [references/reply-playbook.md](references/reply-playbook.md) for a draft pattern for each class.

### 2. Draft the response
- Answer what they asked first, in their length. A one-line reply gets a short answer.
- Interested: confirm, offer two specific times or the booking link, and one line on what the call will cover.
- Question: answer directly; then the meeting question.
- Objection: acknowledge, one clarifying question, respect the answer.
- Referral: thank them, then contact the referred person naming who suggested it.

### 3. Set the next action
Each reply gets: classification, draft, next step, follow-up date and the CRM update (status, reason, notes).

### 4. Hand over for approval
Group drafts by priority. Unsubscribes are processed immediately (suppression is not a sales message, so it needs no approval to stop sending).

## Output format

```
<prospect> | <class> | priority | draft reply | next step + date | CRM update
```

## What good looks like

- Interested and question replies have drafts ready within minutes.
- Drafts answer the exact question before asking for the meeting.
- "Not now" replies get a dated follow-up, not a lost note.
- The common mistake is answering every positive reply with a calendar link and nothing else, which reads like a bot and drops conversion.

## Rules

- MUST suppress unsubscribes and hostile replies across all channels immediately.
- MUST get approval before sending any drafted reply.
- MUST stop all sequences for anyone who replied.
- NEVER argue with a "not interested".
- NEVER invent pricing, features or availability in an answer.

## Example prompts

- "Here are 37 replies from yesterday's campaign. Classify them and draft responses."
- "They replied 'what does it cost?'. Draft an answer that gets to a meeting."
- "Set up reply categories and templates for our SDR team."

references.title: Reply playbook
references.markdown:
# Reply playbook

## Interested

> Great, thanks Maya. The call is 20 minutes: how your close runs today, what Contoso changed, and whether it would work for you. Does Tuesday at 10 or Wednesday at 2 (your time) work? Or grab any slot here: <booking link>

## Question: price

> Fair question. It depends on the number of entities; most teams your size land between <range from the approved price list>. The 20-minute call is the fastest way to get you an exact number. Tuesday at 10 or Wednesday at 2?

If pricing is public, link to it and give the likely plan in one line.

## Question: how does it work / integrations

Answer in two or three sentences, plainly. Then: "Easier to show than tell. 15 minutes this week?"

## Referral

To the referrer:
> Thanks Tom, appreciated. I'll reach out to Priya and mention you pointed me her way.

To the referred person:
> Hi Priya, Tom suggested I get in touch about month-end close. <one-line problem + proof>. Worth 20 minutes?

## Objection: "We already use something"

> Makes sense. Out of curiosity, how long does close take with it today? If it's under 5 days, you're ahead of most and I'll leave you be.

## Objection: "No budget"

> Understood. When does planning for next year start? Happy to send something useful before then and not chase you in the meantime.

## Not now

> No problem. I'll check back in <month they named>. Anything specific you'd want to see by then?

Then: schedule the follow-up for that date, set the status to nurture.

## Not interested

> Understood, thanks for letting me know. I won't follow up.

Close the record with the reason if given.

## Wrong person

> Thanks for letting me know. Who would be best to talk to about <topic>? Happy to keep your name out of it if you prefer.

## Out of office

No reply. Pause all steps; resume two business days after the return date. If the auto-reply names a delegate, treat as a referral (without naming the out-of-office person as a "recommendation").

## Unsubscribe or hostile

No sales reply. Optional single line: "Done, you won't hear from us again." Suppress on email, domain-level for the person, and LinkedIn.

Use this before a new SDR starts. A structured first month is the difference between first meetings in week three and in week eight.

## Inputs

- Product, ICP, personas and the main plays.
- Sales process, stages and the tools reps use.
- Full-ramp targets (meetings per month) and who coaches.

## The play

### 1. Structure the first 90 days
Read [references/onboarding-plan.md](references/onboarding-plan.md) for the week-by-week plan. The shape:

| Phase | Weeks | Focus | Gate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Learn | 1-2 | ICP, personas, product, process, tools | Certification: ICP and pitch |
| Practice | 2-3 | Messaging, calls, role-plays, shadowing | Certification: role-play pass |
| Ramp | 3-8 | Live outreach with rising targets and daily review | Ramp targets met |
| Own | 9-13 | Full targets, own campaigns, peer coaching | Full quota |

### 2. Teach the buyer before the product
Reps who understand the customer's day, problems and language write better first lines than reps who memorised features.

### 3. Certify, don't assume
Short, real tests: pitch the value proposition in 30 seconds, write three first emails that pass review, handle five common objections in a role-play, qualify a mock discovery call.

### 4. Ramp the targets
Typical ramp for meetings: month 1, 25-35% of full target; month 2, 60-70%; month 3, 100%. Activity starts lower and leans on quality: fewer, better-researched touches.

### 5. Coach on a cadence
Daily 15-minute check-ins for the first four weeks, weekly call or email reviews, and a 30/60/90 review with the manager. Pair each new rep with a buddy who is hitting target.

### 6. Watch the early-warning signals
Not certifying by week 3, low activity quality (emails failing review), avoiding calls, no positive replies by week 5. Act early with extra practice rather than waiting for the month-3 number.

## What good looks like

- The new rep books a first meeting within the first four weeks.
- Certifications use real scenarios, not slide quizzes.
- The plan is a living document with owners for each session.
- The common mistake is two weeks of product slides, then a full activity target from week three.

## Rules

- MUST include certification gates before live outreach.
- MUST set ramped targets, not full targets, for the first two months.
- NEVER let new reps send unreviewed outreach in their first two weeks live.

## Example prompts

- "Build a 90-day onboarding plan for 3 new SDRs selling to HR leaders."
- "Write the certification tests for new BDRs."
- "Our reps take 5 months to ramp. Fix our onboarding."

references.title: SDR onboarding plan, week by week
references.markdown:
# SDR onboarding plan, week by week

## Week 1: the buyer and the business
- Day 1: welcome, tools access, buddy assigned, read the ICP and persona documents.
- Days 2-3: listen to 8-10 recorded calls (good and bad); write down the buyer's words for pains.
- Day 4: product walkthrough focused on the 3 problems customers buy it for.
- Day 5: shadow a senior SDR for a full day; recap what they noticed first on each account.

## Week 2: messaging and process
- Value proposition and messaging matrix; write it back in their own words.
- Sales process, stages, qualification criteria, handoff rules.
- Write 10 first emails and 10 LinkedIn notes; manager reviews line by line.
- **Certification 1**: 30-second pitch per persona; explain the ICP and disqualifiers.

## Week 3: practice
- Daily role-plays: cold call opener, 5 objections, a discovery mini-call.
- Research and tier 30 accounts; present 3 account briefs.
- **Certification 2**: role-play pass on calls and objections; 3 emails pass review.
- First live touches to 20-30 accounts with every message reviewed.

## Weeks 4-8: ramp
| Week | New contacts per week | Review | Target |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | 50 | Every message | First positive reply |
| 5 | 75 | Sample of 10 | First meeting booked |
| 6 | 100 | Sample of 10 | 25-35% of meeting target (month 1) |
| 7-8 | 125-150 | Weekly | On track for 60-70% in month 2 |

Daily 15-minute check-in: yesterday's numbers, one thing that worked, one thing to fix.

## Weeks 9-13: own it
- Full activity and meeting targets.
- Runs one own campaign end to end (list, copy, analysis) with manager sign-off.
- Teaches one session to the next new rep.
- 90-day review: numbers, skills scorecard, development goals.

## Skills scorecard (score 1-4 at days 30, 60, 90)

| Skill | 1 | 4 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ICP judgement | Contacts poor fits | Rarely misses; flags bad lists |
| Research | Generic openers | Sourced, relevant hooks quickly |
| Writing | Long, about us | Short, about them, passes review first time |
| Calls | Reads script | Conversational, handles objections |
| Reply handling | Slow, generic | Same-day, books from questions |
| Self-management | Needs reminders | Plans own day, hits activity |

Use this when a target meets the limits of safe sending. It answers whether the goal is reachable, what infrastructure it needs, and how long until it runs at full speed.

## Inputs

- Monthly meeting goal.
- Conversion rates from recent campaigns (or the defaults below, labelled as assumptions).
- Channels in use and per-account safe limits.

## The play

### 1. Work backwards
```
Meetings needed per month: M
÷ meeting rate from positive replies (default 50%)  = positive replies
÷ positive reply rate per contact (default 1.5%)    = contacts per month
× touches per contact (email steps)                 = emails per month
÷ working days (21)                                 = emails per day
```

Example: 40 meetings ÷ 0.5 = 80 positive replies ÷ 0.015 = 5,333 contacts × 4 emails = 21,333 emails a month ÷ 21 = about 1,016 emails a day.

### 2. Size email infrastructure
Mailboxes = daily emails ÷ 30 (a conservative per-mailbox cold volume). Domains = mailboxes ÷ 3. Add 20% spare.
Example: 1,016 ÷ 30 = 34 mailboxes → 41 with spare, across about 14 domains.

### 3. Size LinkedIn
Per account: about 15-25 invitations a day, so roughly 100 a week. If LinkedIn carries part of the load, divide contacts between channels and size accounts accordingly. Each account must belong to a real person on the team.

### 4. Check the list can feed it
5,333 new contacts a month is about 64,000 a year. Compare with the SAM: if the ICP has 20,000 reachable contacts, the plan exhausts it in four months. That is the real bottleneck, and the fix is better conversion, not more mailboxes.

### 5. Show ramp and cost
New mailboxes need 4-6 weeks to reach full volume. Show month by month capacity and the monthly cost of domains and mailboxes.

### 6. Name the bottleneck
Usually one of: list size (SAM), reply rate (copy and targeting), meeting conversion (reply handling speed), or infrastructure. Raising positive reply rate from 1.5% to 3% halves every number above.

## Output format

```
Goal: M meetings/month
Funnel: contacts N → positive replies N → meetings M (rates used, assumed or measured)
Email: N/day → N mailboxes, N domains (incl. spare)
LinkedIn: N accounts (if used)
List check: N contacts/month vs SAM N → months of runway
Ramp: month 1 X%, month 2 Y%, full from week 6
Bottleneck: <one thing to fix first>
```

## What good looks like

- Every rate is labelled measured or assumed.
- The plan checks list supply, not only sending capacity.
- The common mistake is solving a 0.5% reply rate with 50 more mailboxes; volume multiplies whatever the conversion is, including burned contacts.

## Rules

- MUST use conservative per-mailbox and per-account limits.
- MUST check the plan against the size of the reachable market.
- NEVER plan LinkedIn capacity on fake or shared profiles.

## Example prompts

- "We need 30 meetings a month from outbound. How many mailboxes and LinkedIn accounts?"
- "Here are our real conversion rates. Is 60 meetings a month realistic?"
- "Plan our sending capacity for next quarter and tell me the bottleneck."

Use this before any page is written for search. A good brief makes the writer's job specific: who it is for, what it must answer better than what ranks today, and what the reader should do next.

## Inputs

- The target keyword or topic.
- Product, audience and the problem it connects to.
- Existing pages on the site (to link and avoid cannibalising).

## The play

### 1. Read the intent
Look at what ranks today and classify the intent: informational (how to, what is), commercial (best, vs, alternatives, tools), transactional (pricing, template, free tool) or navigational. The format of the top results is the format searchers expect; fight it only with a reason.

### 2. Find the gap
For the top results, note what they cover, how deep they go, what they miss, and how fresh they are. Your page wins on one of: depth, original data, a better tool or template, expert experience, or clearer structure.

### 3. Choose angle and format
One sentence: "The <format> that <does what the others don't> for <audience>."

### 4. Build the outline
Read [references/brief-template.md](references/brief-template.md) for the full template. It covers:
- Title tag (under 60 characters) and meta description (under 155).
- H1 and H2/H3 structure, each with what it must say.
- Questions to answer (from search suggestions and buyer calls), each answered in the first sentence of its section.
- Entities and terms that should appear naturally.
- Original value: data, examples, screenshots, templates.
- Internal links to and from the page; schema (FAQ, HowTo, SoftwareApplication, Article).
- The conversion path: a CTA that fits the intent (template download, free tool, demo for commercial intent).

### 5. Set success metrics
Target position and traffic, plus what matters more: sign-ups, demo requests or assisted pipeline from the page.

## What good looks like

- The brief says exactly why this page will be better than what ranks.
- Every heading has a job; no "Introduction" or "Conclusion" sections.
- Answers lead each section (good for featured snippets and AI answers).
- The CTA matches the intent: nobody searching "what is an ICP" wants a demo.
- The common mistake is a brief that is a keyword list plus "write 2,000 words", which produces the same page as everyone else.

## Rules

- MUST base the outline on actual intent and the current results.
- MUST include something original (data, template, expert view, example).
- NEVER target a keyword an existing page already covers without a consolidation plan.
- NEVER recommend keyword stuffing, doorway pages or fake reviews.

## Example prompts

- "Write an SEO brief for 'cold email templates for SaaS'."
- "Brief a comparison page for 'Acme alternatives'."
- "Plan a cluster of 8 pages around 'sales prospecting'."

references.markdown:
# SEO brief template

```
Keyword: <primary>           Secondary: <3-6 variants>
Intent: informational / commercial / transactional
Audience: <role, situation>
Angle: "The <format> that <difference> for <audience>"
Format: guide / list / template / tool / comparison / landing page
Length guide: <range, set by what it takes to answer, not by competitors>

Title tag (≤60): <...>
Meta description (≤155): <...>
URL: /<short-slug>/
H1: <...>

Outline:
H2 <section> - must say: <one line> - answer first sentence: <...>
  H3 <...>
H2 ...

Questions to answer: <5-10, each mapped to a section>
Entities and terms: <...>
Original value: <data / template / screenshots / expert quote>
Internal links out: <3-6 pages with anchor text>
Internal links in: <pages that should link here>
Schema: <FAQPage / HowTo / Article / SoftwareApplication>
CTA: <primary + placement> | Secondary: <...>
Success: <rank target, traffic, conversions>
Refresh: <when to review>
```

## Intent to CTA map

| Intent | Example query | Fitting CTA |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Informational | "what is lead scoring" | Template or checklist download |
| How-to | "how to warm up a domain" | Free tool or step-by-step checklist |
| Commercial list | "best cold email tools" | Comparison table, free trial |
| Comparison | "x vs y", "x alternatives" | Side-by-side, migration help, demo |
| Transactional | "cold email template" | Instant copy, then a related product CTA |

## Writing rules to hand the writer

- Answer the section's question in the first sentence; then explain.
- Use the reader's terms; define jargon once.
- Short paragraphs, tables for comparisons, numbered steps for processes.
- Real examples and numbers beat adjectives.
- Date-sensitive facts carry a "last checked" note in the brief so they get refreshed.

Use this when LinkedIn activity is sporadic: a burst of posting, then nothing for a month. It produces a routine short enough to keep and specific enough to measure.

## Inputs

- Target accounts and personas.
- Time available per day.
- Current activity: posts per week, connections, messages, replies.

## The play

### 1. The daily block (30-45 minutes)
| Minutes | Activity | Target |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5 | Check notifications; reply to comments and messages | Every reply within the day |
| 10 | Comment on 5-8 posts from target buyers and the voices they follow | 5+ thoughtful comments |
| 10 | Send connection requests with notes to today's list | 10-20 requests |
| 10 | First messages to new connections; follow-ups due today | All due messages |
| 5 | Log meetings, replies and anything worth a post | Updated sheet |

### 2. The weekly layer
- 2 posts a week (one practical, one story or opinion).
- Refresh the target list: add 50-100 new people, remove those who declined or went cold.
- 30-minute review on Friday (below).

### 3. Track five numbers
Connection requests sent, acceptance rate, conversations started (replies), meetings booked, and posts published. Followers and impressions are vanity unless the right people are in them.

### 4. Weekly review
| If | Then |
| --- | --- |
| Acceptance under 25% | Tighten targeting or fix the profile and note |
| Accepted but few replies | First message is a pitch; make it a question about their world |
| Replies but no meetings | Bridge to the problem earlier; offer something concrete |
| Posts get likes from peers, not buyers | Write about buyer problems, not your industry gossip |

### 5. Protect the account
Stay well inside invitation and message limits, avoid browser extensions that automate actions in ways the platform prohibits, and keep pending invitations under a few hundred by withdrawing old ones.

## What good looks like

- Done four or five days a week for a quarter, not seven days for two weeks.
- The numbers move: acceptance, conversations and meetings, in that order.
- The common mistake is treating posting as the whole strategy; most meetings come from conversations, which come from connecting and commenting.

## Rules

- MUST keep activity inside safe platform limits.
- MUST review the numbers weekly and change one thing at a time.
- NEVER buy followers, engagement pods or fake engagement.

## Example prompts

- "Build me a 30-minute daily LinkedIn routine. I'm a founder selling to HR leaders."
- "Review my last month of LinkedIn numbers and tell me what to change."
- "Make a tracking sheet for my team's social selling."

Use this after the email is written. The subject line's job is to get the email opened by the right person without promising something the body does not deliver.

## Inputs

- The email body (subject lines are written for a specific email, never in a vacuum).
- The persona and seniority.
- The trigger or angle the email uses.

## The play

### 1. Write in the patterns that work for cold B2B
| Pattern | Example | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Topic, two to four words | "month-end close" | Default |
| Trigger reference | "new sdr team", "the series b" | Email leads with a trigger |
| Peer or customer | "contoso's close" | Strong, approved proof |
| Question | "manual reconciliations?" | Pain is very common |
| Their initiative | "europe expansion" | Announced plan |
| Mutual context (only if real) | "maria suggested i reach out" | Genuine referral |

### 2. Follow the format rules
- 1 to 5 words; under 40 characters so it is not cut on phones.
- Lowercase or sentence case; it should look like it came from a colleague.
- No first-name merge field in the subject (it reads as automated), no emojis, no exclamation marks, no "quick question".
- The subject must be true to the email. Clickbait wins opens and loses replies and trust.

### 3. Give options per pattern
Return 2-3 options for 3 patterns. Mark the recommended one.

### 4. Test fairly
- Change only the subject; keep body, list and send time the same.
- At least 200 sends per variant before judging.
- Judge on reply rate, not opens. Open tracking is unreliable: privacy features pre-load images and inflate opens, and many teams disable tracking pixels to protect deliverability.

## Output format

```
Recommended: <subject>
Topic: <3 options>
Trigger: <3 options>
Question: <3 options>
Avoid: <any risky phrasing found and why>
Test: A = <..>, B = <..>, judge on reply rate after 200+ sends each
```

## What good looks like

- Reads like a peer's email in a crowded inbox.
- Connects directly to the first line of the email.
- No spam-pattern words: "free", "guarantee", "act now", "limited time", percentages off.
- The common mistake is clever or vague subjects ("thoughts?", "a crazy idea") that get opened out of curiosity and then deleted with irritation.

## Rules

- MUST keep subject lines under 40 characters.
- MUST match the subject to the email's actual content.
- NEVER use fake reply or forward prefixes ("Re:", "Fwd:") on a first email.
- NEVER use a referral subject unless the referral is real.

## Example prompts

- "Write subject lines for this cold email to CFOs."
- "Give me 10 subject lines for a follow-up that shares a case study."
- "Set up a subject line test for our new campaign."

Use this when someone asks "how big is the market?" or "do we have enough accounts?". It produces a bottom-up size that survives questions, because every number traces to a count or a price.

## Inputs

- ICP and the segments you sell to.
- Pricing and the average first-year contract value per segment.
- Account counts per segment from a company database, industry registry or association data. Estimates are acceptable if labelled.

## The play

### 1. Count accounts, do not quote reports
Top-down numbers ("the sales software market is $X billion") cannot be worked and rarely survive diligence. Start from countable companies: headcount band × industry × region.

### 2. Define the three layers
- **TAM**: every account that could use the product at full price, globally.
- **SAM**: accounts you can serve today: regions, languages, integrations and segments you support.
- **SOM**: accounts you can realistically win in 3 years given team size, win rates and sales capacity.

### 3. Price each segment
Accounts × annual contract value. Use real deal data per segment; a blended average hides that enterprise accounts are 10x the value and 3x the cycle length.

### 4. Pressure-test SOM with capacity
SOM must be reachable by the go-to-market you have or plan to fund. Capacity check: reps × accounts each can work per year × win rate. If capacity reaches 400 wins and SOM says 4,000, SOM is wrong. Read [references/sizing-worked-example.md](references/sizing-worked-example.md) for the full table.

### 5. Check outbound coverage
Divide SAM accounts by the number of reps and by contacts touched per rep per quarter. If a team will exhaust its SAM in under 4 quarters, flag it: list fatigue is coming and the ICP needs widening or new channels.

## Output format

```
Segment table: segment | accounts | ACV | TAM $ | in SAM? | SOM share | SOM $
Totals: TAM $X (N accounts) | SAM $Y (N) | SOM $Z (N) in 3 years
Assumptions: <each with source or "estimate">
Capacity check: <reps x accounts x win rate = wins/year>
Coverage: <quarters until SAM is fully touched at current volume>
Biggest uncertainty: <one line + how to reduce it>
```

## What good looks like

- Every number in the deck can be traced to a row in the assumption table.
- SOM is constrained by capacity, not by ambition. "1% of a huge market" is the classic red flag investors look for.
- Segments are separated, because the decision the sizing supports is usually "which segment first".
- The best version ends with an account list size, not just a dollar figure, so sales can act on it.

## Rules

- MUST build bottom-up from account counts and prices.
- MUST label every estimate as an estimate.
- NEVER present a top-down analyst figure as your TAM without the bottom-up check.
- NEVER let SOM exceed what the sales capacity check supports.

## Example prompts

- "Size the market for our payroll tool for restaurant groups in the US and UK."
- "Build TAM, SAM and SOM for our seed deck, bottom-up, with every assumption shown."
- "We have 6 SDRs. Do we have enough accounts in our SAM for the next two years?"

references.title: Sizing worked example
references.markdown:
# Sizing worked example

Product: scheduling software for multi-location dental groups. Illustrative numbers.

## Segment table

| Segment | Accounts | ACV | TAM | In SAM | SOM share (3 yrs) | SOM |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| US groups, 5-20 locations | 3,100 | $18,000 | $55.8M | Yes | 8% | $4.5M |
| US groups, 21-100 locations | 640 | $60,000 | $38.4M | Yes | 6% | $2.3M |
| US groups, 100+ locations | 85 | $220,000 | $18.7M | No (needs SSO, not built) | 0% | $0 |
| UK groups, 5+ locations | 520 | $16,000 | $8.3M | Yes | 4% | $0.3M |
| Rest of world | 4,000 (estimate) | $15,000 | $60.0M | No | 0% | $0 |
| **Total** | **8,345** | | **$181.2M** | **$102.5M** | | **$7.1M** |

## Assumption table

| Assumption | Value | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| US group counts | 3,100 / 640 / 85 | Industry association membership data |
| ACV by segment | $18k / $60k / $220k | Our closed-won averages; the 100+ figure is an estimate from 3 deals |
| UK count | 520 | Company registry search, SIC code + location count |
| Rest of world | 4,000 | Estimate, low confidence |
| SOM share | 4-8% | Current win rate × reachable accounts, see capacity check |

## Capacity check

- 4 AEs, each can run 60 qualified opportunities a year.
- Win rate 25%.
- Wins per year: 4 × 60 × 0.25 = 60. Over 3 years with hiring to 8 AEs: about 270 wins.
- SOM accounts implied by the table: 248 + 38 + 21 = 307. Close to capacity, so SOM holds. If it had implied 1,000 accounts, it would need cutting.

## Coverage check

- SAM accounts: 4,260. Contacts per account: 3. Total: about 12,800 contacts.
- 3 SDRs each start 600 new contacts a month: 1,800 a month.
- Months to touch the full SAM once: about 7. The team will need re-engagement plays and the 100+ segment (SSO) within a year.

Use this when the company cannot say what it does in a sentence that makes a buyer lean in. It produces one value proposition and the versions each channel needs.

## Inputs

- The product and who uses it.
- Evidence: customer quotes, win reasons, reviews, the words buyers use on calls.
- Alternatives: competitors, spreadsheets, agencies, hiring, doing nothing.

## The play

### 1. Start with the alternative, not the product
What does the buyer do today without you? The value proposition is the difference between that and life with you. Read [references/value-prop-canvas.md](references/value-prop-canvas.md) for the canvas and a worked example.

### 2. Find the outcome only you deliver
List the outcomes customers mention. Strike every outcome a competitor could claim with a straight face. What is left is your positioning; if nothing is left, the differentiation is in the how (speed, simplicity, a segment you serve better), so say that.

### 3. Write the one-liner
Formula options:
- "<Outcome> for <who>, without <the pain of the alternative>."
- "<Product> helps <who> <do the job> so they can <outcome>."
- "The <category> for <specific who>."

Test: a buyer should be able to repeat it to a colleague after hearing it once.

### 4. Back it with three pillars
Each pillar: a benefit headline, how it works in one line, and proof (a number, a customer, a demo moment).

### 5. Write channel versions
- Homepage: headline (under 10 words), subheadline (one sentence), three pillars.
- Cold email: one sentence, in the reader's problem language.
- Sales call: a 30-second spoken version.
- LinkedIn headline or bio.

## Output format

```
One-liner: <...>
Paragraph (40-60 words): <...>
Pillars: <benefit - how - proof> x3
Homepage: H1 / subhead
```

references.title: Value proposition canvas
references.markdown:
# Value proposition canvas

## The canvas

| Box | Question | Answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who | Which buyer, at which kind of company, in which situation? | |
| Job | What are they trying to get done? | |
| Today | How do they do it now (the alternative)? | |
| Pain | What is costly, slow, risky or annoying about today? | |
| Outcome | What does success look like, in their words? | |
| Unique | Why can only we deliver it this way? | |
| Proof | What evidence supports it? | |

## Worked example: scheduling for multi-location dental groups

| Box | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Who | Operations leaders at dental groups with 10-60 locations |
| Job | Fill every chair every day across locations |
| Today | Each location schedules on its own; the ops team stitches it together in spreadsheets |
| Pain | Empty chairs at one site while another turns patients away; Monday reports are already out of date |
| Outcome | "I can see and fill every chair across the group from one screen" |
| Unique | Group-level schedule that moves patients and staff across nearby locations automatically |
| Proof | Northwind Dental: chair utilisation from 71% to 86% in 90 days |

One-liner: "Fill every chair across every location, without the Monday spreadsheet."

Paragraph: "Dental groups lose revenue when one office is overbooked and the next one sits empty. <Product> puts every location's schedule in one view and moves patients and staff to where there is capacity. Northwind Dental went from 71% to 86% chair utilisation in 90 days."

## Phrases to replace

| Instead of | Say |
| --- | --- |
| All-in-one platform | What it replaces: "your scheduling spreadsheet and three portals" |
| AI-powered | What the AI does: "suggests the best open slot nearby" |
| Streamline workflows | The specific time saved: "Monday reporting takes 10 minutes" |
| Best-in-class | The proof: a customer and a number |
| Enterprise-grade | The specific thing: "SSO, audit logs, data stays in the region" |

Use this for Tier 1 accounts where a short video can show, not tell. A personalised video works when the first seconds prove it was made for this person; it fails when it is a generic demo with their name in the title.

## Inputs

- Research on the person and account.
- What to show on screen: their website, a post, a job listing, a dashboard example, a before and after.
- Offer and one proof point.

## The play

### 1. Plan the first five seconds
Open with their name and something of theirs on screen. The thumbnail shows it too: their homepage, their post, a whiteboard with their name. The first five seconds decide whether they keep watching.

### 2. Script it in four beats (45-75 seconds)
| Beat | Seconds | Content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hook | 0-8 | "Hi Maya, made this for you. This is Lumen's careers page..." |
| Observation | 8-25 | What you noticed and why it matters for them |
| Insight | 25-50 | One idea or a peer example, shown on screen |
| Ask | 50-65 | Easy next step, said and repeated in the email |

### 3. Write the carrier email
Short, with the thumbnail as an image linking to the video (a GIF or image of the first frame works; embedded players do not render in most inboxes). Subject: "made this for you, Maya" or the topic.

### 4. Record fast, not perfect
One or two takes. Natural beats polished. Look at the camera during the hook and the ask.

## Example script

> [Screen: Lumen careers page, four SDR listings highlighted]
>
> "Hi Dana, I made this quick video for you. This is your careers page: four SDR roles, all saying outbound is being built from scratch.
>
> [Screen: simple timeline of a new SDR's first month]
>
> Here's what usually happens to new SDR teams: weeks one to four go to building lists and researching accounts, so first meetings land in week six.
>
> [Screen: a peer's anonymised before and after]
>
> Northwind changed one thing: each rep got a researched list on day one. First meetings moved to week two.
>
> If that's useful before your new hires start, reply 'yes' and I'll send you how they set it up. Thanks Dana."

## What good looks like

- Their world is on screen in the first frame.
- Under 75 seconds; one idea.
- The ask is a one-word reply, not a meeting.
- The common mistake is a two-minute product demo with "Hi <name>" stitched on the front.

## Rules

- MUST show something specific to the prospect in the first seconds.
- MUST keep videos under 90 seconds for cold outreach.
- NEVER show other customers' confidential data on screen; anonymise or use approved examples.

## Example prompts

- "Write a 60-second video script for the CRO at Fabrikam. They just opened an EMEA office."
- "Turn this cold email into a video script with screen directions."
- "Write a video recap to send after today's discovery call."

Use this when a call goes to voicemail or when a LinkedIn voice note could stand out. Callbacks are rare; the real job of a voicemail is to make your next email or message recognised and opened.

## Inputs

- The situation: cold, follow-up to an email, referral, no-show, post-event.
- The email or message it pairs with.
- The prospect's name and the problem.

## The play

### 1. Keep the structure
1. Name and company (2 seconds).
2. One reason, tied to their situation (8-10 seconds).
3. What happens next: "I'll send you a short note today with the subject <x>" (5 seconds).
4. Number twice, slowly, only if a callback is realistic (5 seconds).

15-25 seconds total. Longer voicemails get deleted before the point.

### 2. Pair it with a written touch
Always send the email or message within an hour, and reference the voicemail in it ("Left you a quick voicemail about...").

### 3. Scripts by situation

**Cold, paired with an email**
> "Hi Maya, Sam from Acme. I work with finance leads whose month-end close drags because of approvals. I'm sending you a short note today, subject 'month-end close', with how Contoso got to 4 days. That's it, have a good day."

**Referral**
> "Hi Tom, Sam from Acme. Priya Shah suggested I reach out about your scheduling rollout. I'll email you a couple of times that might work. My number is 555 0134, again 555 0134."

**No-show**
> "Hi Ana, Sam here, we had 2 o'clock booked. No problem at all, I know days get away. I'll send a link to pick a new time that suits you."

**LinkedIn voice note (after a connection accepts)**
> "Hey Dev, thanks for connecting. Your post about ramping SDRs got me curious: do your new reps build their own lists, or does someone hand them accounts on day one? No pitch, genuinely curious how you run it."

### 4. Delivery
Stand up, smile, speak slower than feels natural, say the name correctly (check pronunciation if unsure), and record the voice note again if it sounds read.

## What good looks like

- Under 25 seconds, one reason, a clear next step.
- The paired email arrives the same day.
- The common mistake is the 60-second voicemail that pitches the product and lists features.

## Rules

- MUST keep voicemails under 30 seconds.
- MUST send the paired written touch.
- NEVER leave misleading voicemails that imply an existing relationship or an urgent account issue.

## Example prompts

- "Write voicemails for my 3-call cadence to IT directors."
- "Give me a LinkedIn voice note script for new connections who are VPs of Sales."
- "Write a voicemail for a prospect who missed our meeting."

Use this when company-level website visit data is available. A visit tells you timing and topic; the message must use both without revealing either.

## Inputs

- Company-level visit data: company, pages, number of visits, dates.
- ICP and tiers.
- A map of your site pages to topics and intent level.

## The play

### 1. Map pages to intent
| Page type | Intent | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pricing, plans, demo, contact | High | /pricing, /demo |
| Comparisons and alternatives | High | /vs-competitor |
| Case studies, integrations, security | Medium-high | /customers, /security |
| Product and solution pages | Medium | /product/scheduling |
| Blog, free tools, careers | Low | /blog/*, /careers |

Careers-page visits are usually job seekers; exclude them. Repeat visits by your own customers are product usage, not intent.

### 2. Score and filter
Score = page intent + visit depth (3+ pages: +) + recency (last 48 hours: +) + repeat visits across days (+). Keep only ICP accounts with no open deal owned by someone else and no current customer status.

### 3. Find the likely person
Match the topic to a persona: pricing plus security pages suggests an evaluator in IT or operations; comparison pages suggest the champion. Pick 1-2 people, not the whole company.

### 4. Write about the topic, never the visit
The message offers something useful on the exact topic they looked at: the comparison, the security pack, a pricing explainer, a customer story in their industry. It should read as well-timed, not watched.

> Subject: scheduling for multi-site teams
>
> Hi Ana, teams running 10+ locations usually ask us the same three questions before switching: how shift swaps work, what it costs per location, and how long rollout takes. Here is a two-minute answer to all three. Happy to walk your team through it if useful.

### 5. Move fast, once
High-intent accounts get a touch within 24 hours. One signal-led touch per account per week, then let the normal sequence take over.

## What good looks like

- Zero mentions of the visit, the pages or tracking, in any message.
- The offered asset matches the pages viewed.
- Low-intent blog traffic is left to marketing, not sent to reps.
- The common mistake is "I noticed someone from your company was on our site", which turns a warm signal into a privacy complaint.

## Rules

- MUST work from company-level data and lawful sources only.
- MUST respect the site's consent settings and regional privacy rules.
- NEVER reference the visit, the pages or the tracking in outreach.
- NEVER treat a single blog visit as a reason for sales outreach.

## Example prompts

- "Here are yesterday's identified visitor companies with pages. Who should we contact and what should we send?"
- "Build an intent score for our site's pages."
- "Write follow-ups for accounts that viewed our comparison pages this week."

Use this quarterly or after a run of losses. It replaces anecdotes ("we always lose on price") with patterns and specific changes.

## Inputs

- Closed-won and closed-lost deals for the period with stage lost, reason, competitor, amount, segment and cycle length.
- Call notes, emails and, ideally, 5-10 buyer interviews.
- Rep notes on why they think deals went the way they did.

## The play

### 1. Quantify first
Win rate by segment, deal size, lead source, competitor, rep and stage lost. The stage where deals die says more than the reason field: losses after the demo are fit or value problems; losses after the proposal are price, champion or competitor problems.

### 2. Separate stated from real reasons
"Price" is the most common stated reason and often not the real one. Look for evidence: was the economic buyer engaged? Was value quantified? Did the champion go quiet? Real reasons usually fall into: no quantified value, wrong buyer, competitor better fit, poor timing, weak process, product gap.

### 3. Interview buyers
Short calls with won and lost buyers, run by someone other than the rep. Ask about their process and alternatives, not about the rep. A guide:
- What problem were you trying to solve, and why then?
- What alternatives did you consider, including doing nothing?
- What mattered most in the decision?
- Where did we fall short, or stand out?
- What almost made you choose differently?

### 4. Find patterns
A pattern needs 3+ deals pointing the same way. Group into: targeting, messaging, product, pricing, sales process, competition.

### 5. Turn patterns into changes
Each pattern gets one recommended change, an owner and how to measure it next quarter.

## Output format

```
Period: <dates> | Deals: N won, N lost | Win rate: X% (vs X% last period)
Where we win: <segments, use cases, competitors>
Where we lose: <same, with the stage deals die>
Stated vs real reasons: <table>
Patterns (3+ deals each): <pattern - evidence - change - owner - metric>
Quick wins: <changes that can start next week>
```

## What good looks like

- Losses are explained with evidence from the deal, not from the reason picklist.
- Wins are analysed too; knowing why you win tells you where to aim.
- Recommendations name a team and a metric.
- The common mistake is concluding "we need to be cheaper" from picklist data when the losses show no economic buyer was ever met.

## Rules

- MUST quantify before interpreting.
- MUST treat stated reasons as hypotheses until evidence supports them.
- NEVER single out individual reps in a team-wide report; give rep-level findings privately to managers.
- NEVER share interview quotes with identifying details without the buyer's permission.

## Example prompts

- "Here are 80 closed deals from last quarter. Run a win-loss analysis."
- "Why do we keep losing to Acme in mid-market? Notes attached."
- "Write a win-loss interview guide and a request email to lost buyers."
